📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Netflix at QConSF 2026: Retrofitting the SDLC for AI Coding Agents.

Nov 23, 2026 3 min read.

At QCon San Francisco 2026, Mark Khuzam, senior software engineer at Netflix, described how the organization's Commerce team retrofitted its software development lifecycle so that AI coding agents and engineers could ship together safely.

Khuzam argued that most of the work was not about agents at all, but about documentation, consistency and review.

Much of Commerce runs as server-driven UI, an approach Netflix has discussed at QCon before. A single screen-composition service behind the API gateway builds screens for iOS, Android, web and TV.

Khuzam opened with a mock company email announcing that every engineer now had Claude Code and asking how much faster everyone was shipping. The problem the team ran into next was summed up in one line.

The team's first attempt was having an agent migrate tests, and it took four tries. The team started with "migrate this file," then added instructions, then the APIs to use, then how to mock data.

According to recent reports, the docs were also hard to find, since the agent's context window ran out before it found the right page. And they were inconsistent, because tests were not written the same way across the codebase.

Developers rated the internal framework at a Net Promoter Score of -3. Moving from one test to a whole feature, from screen to data to route to test, meant teaching the agent how the team builds.

Khuzam described the fix as context engineering, "getting what engineers know into what agents see." The team wrote 45 architecture decision records, each "written for people and for agents.".

Each record covers the context, the decision, a pattern and an anti-pattern, and AI usage notes on what an agent should do. It also links to related docs and code, and the records now ship inside almost every repository.

To keep those records and more than 300 other documents findable, the team borrowed from how search engines read a site. An AGENTS.md file, the project instructions file that coding agents read before anything else, plays the part of robots.txt.

The second half of the talk followed code after an agent writes it. Khuzam noted that the CI pipeline is still deterministic, running builds, tests, screenshot diffing, merge queues and canaries.

What changed is how agents plug into each phase. A review agent pre-reviews each pull request against the docs and ADRs, flags anti-patterns and looks at what depends on the change.

Its first version left 23 comments on a single PR, starting with "Overall this PR looks great!" It now posts only verified blockers, each with evidence, a fix and the ADR rule it breaks. Engineers can add a revise label to have an agent read the review and push a fix to the same PR. Changes aren't yet auto-merged, and engineers own the code.

Industry observers note that khuzam reported no Sev 1 incidents in 2026 on a core service and 32% more pull requests year over year. Developer NPS rose from -3 to +25 over three quarters.

Ahead of the session, Khuzam framed the stakes on LinkedIn: "Agents can write code, but what gives us the confidence to ship Tier 0 services to 300M+ members without everything falling apart?".

Sources indicate that work that crosses services raised a harder question. A product engineer building one feature touches the payment API, billing, the gateway and every client, so the team had to decide who owns the context and how it follows the work.

In a recent development, khuzam listed approaches that did not hold up. Loading every repository did not fit, Git submodules were brittle, a Git MCP server "sees one file, not the system," and shared copies went stale.

Recent findings suggest that the team needed context that was accurate, portable across agents, owned per domain and kept fresh. It settled on GraphRAG per domain, taking structure from the code and meaning from the docs and ADRs.

Industry observers note that each graph is pinned to specific commits and served through a single Model Context Protocol tool. Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, a Slack bot and CI review all query the same graph, and every answer cites a file and a line.

Khuzam closed with three rules: decide what agents should do and tell them, make it easy to find how to do it, and remember that human judgement still matters. "None of this is latest. It's good engineering, built for a new reader.".

Developers interested in learning more can watch InfoQ in the coming weeks for video of the session and can view the session details here.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chip boss gets his old job back, but Washington isn't done investigating one of his former flame's businesses.
  • Jensen Huang was barely back in charge of Nvidia when Uncle Sam slapped Megaspeed –­ the Singaporean cloud provider at the center of the scandal that cost him his job ­­– on its trade blacklist.
  • The US Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has added Megaspeed and a number of affiliated businesses to its Entity List, restricting their access to American technology amid an ongoing investigation into the suspected diversion of advanced GPUs to China.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chip boss gets his old job back, but Washington isn't done investigating one of his former flame's businesses.

Jensen Huang was barely back in charge of Nvidia when Uncle Sam slapped Megaspeed –­ the Singaporean cloud provider at the center of the scandal that cost him his job ­­– on its trade blacklist.

The US Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has added Megaspeed and a number of affiliated businesses to its Entity List, restricting their access to American technology amid an ongoing investigation into the suspected diversion of advanced GPUs to China.

The final rule [PDF], filed Monday afternoon and scheduled for publication in the Federal Register on Wednesday, names seven businesses across Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand, including Megaspeed's owner, Swiftdata, and Malaysian subsidiary Speedmatrix.

Also in Washington's crosshairs is Apex Enterprise Solutions, a Singapore-based subsidiary of Chinese cloud computing giant Alibaba.

BIS said the businesses posed a significant risk of diverting advanced computing hardware to recipients or applications not authorized by the US government. Anyone looking to supply the seven companies with goods subject to US export controls will need a license, with applications subject to a "presumption of denial.".

Despite the timing of Monday's announcement, the US government's interest in Megaspeed predates the revelations about Jensen Huang's private life by some considerable margin.

In a joint statement issued last week, the Departments of Justice and Commerce confirmed that the latter had opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 after spotting suspicious activity while monitoring potential violations of semiconductor export controls.

In a recent development, investigators requested records from Nvidia relating to both direct and indirect sales to Megaspeed in May 2025, and the GPU giant put the Singaporean outfit on its internal "no sell" list the following month. US investigators, accompanied by Singaporean law enforcement officials, subsequently visited Megaspeed's premises and interviewed its then-CEO, Alice Huang.

The Justice Department has since taken the lead on the criminal investigation.

Recent findings suggest that alice Huang, who is not related to the Nvidia boss, is a businesswoman with whom Jensen was remarked to be having an affair – he admitted to extramarital infidelity earlier this month, although he never name-checked the Megaspeed exec. According to reports, US intelligence officials suspected she was working on behalf of Chinese intelligence, though Beijing has rejected the espionage allegations.

According to recent reports, megaspeed maintains that its business is lawful and claims Alice Huang formally left the company in August last year. It has also enlisted outside lawyers to conduct an internal investigation.

It has been revealed that nvidia's own Huang lasted all of 11 days in corporate exile. The chipmaker's board unanimously voted to reinstate its co-founder as president and CEO on Monday, less than a week after board chairman Harvey Jones indicated that bringing him back wasn't on the cards.

The U-turn followed a lobbying campaign by some of Silicon Valley's biggest names, including Elon Musk, and some rather more consequential intervention from the White House. President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had personally persuaded Nvidia's directors to give Huang his job back.

Nvidia's board said it had received assurances from senior US government officials regarding the national security implications of Huang's return.

There are still plenty of people in Washington who have questions for Huang, however. The Nvidia boss is due to sit down with three congressional committees on December 1, with the chipmaker's general counsel, Tim Teter, scheduled to face lawmakers the following day.

Nvidia has also established a board-level committee to oversee national security and export control compliance, putting its trade compliance personnel under the supervision of three directors.

Nvidia shareholders may be delighted to have Jensen back, but the returning CEO has barely a week to prepare for his congressional grilling over the affair that helped bring about his departure. ®.

tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

📅 21 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1582 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows.
  • As models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift.
  • It has been revealed that this is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows. Compute-wise, tokenization is light compared to the heavy modeling happening in the rest of the pipeline. Yet, in some cases, it has rapidly become key to accelerating (or slowing down) your machine learning work.

As models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift. Training on massive datasets, serving many concurrent requests, or repeatedly processing long inputs can put enough pressure on the tokenizer that it starves the model of data.

It has been revealed that this is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers. Tokenization should be light and should scale with your workflow. Your GPUs should never sit idle waiting for the CPU to complete its tokenization.

In this article, we look at what makes v1 faster than v0.23, often by tens of times.

In a recent development, this work was entirely possible thanks to the rest of the ecosystem. Tokenization is a very active area of open source work, and libraries such as gigatoken, tiktoken, kitoken, tokie, fastokens, wordchipper and ai-tokenizer, as well as many others, have each pushed on what a fast tokenizer can be. We read that work, and several of the ideas below reached us because another project highlighted they were worth trying.

According to recent reports, before this refactor, tokenizers was nowhere near the performance it could have had, so contributing to it may not have seemed worth it. With this refactor, we hope to make clear that we intend tokenizers to be a library worth contributing to.

We also thank IBM, NVIDIA, and the ExecuTorch team for contributing patches and helping us test across a wide range of hardware to broaden platform support.

Recent findings suggest that we showcase results for the release candidate of tokenizers v1 against other widely used alternatives. We go over single-threaded, multi-threaded, scaling across threads, per-model comparison, per-language comparison, latency, decoding throughput, memory heap, as well as crate size.

We run this from the tokbench repository, and add a command to rerun the benchmarks on your hardware if you would like to do so.

v1 will produce the same token IDs as v0.23. The goal was to preserve the output, the API, the vocabulary and the merge ranks, and improve everything that can be improved. That includes breadth. The library stays general across tokenizer families rather than specialising on BPE, so v1 loads everything v0.23 loaded.

Industry observers note that A tokenizer converts text into the list of integers a model reads. tokenizers runs that conversion in four stages. Normalization applies operations such as lowercasing or Unicode normalization to the raw text. Pre-tokenization splits the text into smaller pieces called pre-tokens. The model turns each pre-token into tokens and maps them to IDs in its vocabulary. Post-processing adds any special tokens the model expects.

In a recent development, the model stage is where most of the work described here happens. Eight of the ten model families measured in this article use byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from the bytes of a pre-token and repeatedly joins the highest ranked adjacent pair until no ranked pair remains. The ranking is learned when the tokenizer is trained and ships with it, so the same text always produces the same IDs. A merge never crosses a pre-token boundary. The other two families use WordPiece and Unigram, the two other model types the library supports.

The tokenization pipeline page documents the four stages. Tokenization algorithms documents BPE, WordPiece and Unigram.

Each stage was worked on. These are the changes that mattered:.

BPE models use a regular expression to split the input text into smaller, easier to process chunks called pre-tokens. Merges happen inside a pre-token and never across the boundary between two of them, so this split decides what the rest of the pipeline sees.

Recent findings suggest that that regular expression is a fixed parameter of the model. It ships with the tokenizer and never changes at runtime, so there is no need for a general-purpose regex engine to interpret it on every encode. An equivalent splitting function can be written by hand, once, for the pattern a given model actually uses.

A hand-written function can then use the SIMD instructions (single instruction, multiple data) of a modern CPU, which apply one operation to many bytes at once and suit UTF-8 text well. bitcannon views the input's bytes as parallel streams of bits, so boundaries fall out of boolean operations across whole registers instead of a scan that advances one character at a time. It decides 64 bytes per register operation. The same idea drives Parabix for text processing and simdjson for JSON.

This depends on recognising the pattern. A handful of grammars cover most byte-level BPE models, and a tokenizer whose pattern is not among them keeps the regex path and none of this speed-up. That is why the gains above vary as much as they do.

Real text contains many repeated words. Because BPE always produces the same token IDs for a given pre-token, v1 can save the result after processing it once. A thread-local cache maps each pre-token's bytes to its token IDs, allowing later occurrences to skip the merge process.

Recent findings suggest that naturally, as the input grows, the number of unique words can grow more slowly than the total number of words. Repeated words then account for an increasing share of the input. Latest words still appear, which accounts for the occasional misses in the animation below.

Reproduce the shared-prefix result with:.

According to recent reports, caching works best when the input contains repeated pre-tokens. Input with few repeated pre-tokens can pay for lookups without receiving many hits.

The next major cost comes from the BPE merge loop. For each pre-token, the loop repeatedly finds the highest-priority adjacent pair and merges it. The previous implementation allocated fresh memory for every call and built a new priority queue for every pre-token.

Sources indicate that v1 reuses a scratch buffer owned by the caller, removing those repeated allocations. It stores symbols in a flat array and links adjacent symbols by their positions in that array, which makes updates during merging cheaper. It also processes a batch of pre-tokens in a single model call.

In a recent development, each candidate pair is also packed into a single 64-bit value, with the merge rank in the high bits. Comparing two candidates is then just comparing two integers, and "no merge here" is the largest possible value, so the loop finds its next merge without a branch.

It has been revealed that small differences in benchmark design can produce large differences in tokenizer performance. We used the following rules to keep the comparison consistent across engines.

Recent findings suggest that repeatedly encoding one document can be faster than encoding a stream of distinct documents on the same build. The first approach measures performance when the entire document is already represented in the cache. The second measures performance on latest input while allowing previously seen pre-tokens to remain cached.

Both conditions are sometimes described as "warm," even though they measure different workloads. Our headline results use distinct documents, and the complete corpus is too large to fit in the cache. Tokenizer benchmarks should identify which workload they use because the choice can dominate the result.

Across the ten model families v1's encode path covers, it encodes text 3 to 30 times faster than v0.23 with one thread on an Apple M4 Max. The low end is t5-base, the high end gpt2. It scales at 76% of linear across eight workers. Throughout these changes, v1 produces exactly the same token IDs as the released library.

In a recent development, the overall improvement comes from several changes working together: a hand-written splitter in place of a regex engine, a cache that answers a repeated word without merging it again, a merge loop that never touches the allocator, and one model call per batch of pre-tokens instead of one per pre-token. Each reduces the work done at a different point in the pipeline.

The next priority is support for more model families. We will move additional models onto the new merge loop before 1.0.0. Once the release candidates stabilize, the next step will be bringing about the improvements within the transformers library and the rest of the ecosystem which depend on the tokenizers library.

This post is generated from tokbench results and will be updated as support expands.

A release candidate for v1 is on crates.io. The API you call is the one you already call, so the only thing that changes is which build you install.

It has been revealed that training is behind a default-on feature that pulls a C++ dependency with it. If you only need to encode, turn it off to exclude the training implementation:.

Encoding is unchanged: same call, same ids.

According to recent reports, every figure in this post was measured against this crate. The Python bindings wrap the same code and are built from bindings/python, but they add per-call overhead that none of these measurements include.

Sources indicate that the benchmarks in this post cover the completed release-candidate work listed first. The remaining sections show what is still required for 1.0.0 and what we plan to explore afterward.

This work is in the Rust pre-release on crates.io:.

Will have to try it out. Data seems real good.

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (949 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Github ↗ Open Full Page

iTerm2 Arbitrary Command Execution via Kitty Image Protocol APC Response Injection

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (949 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • iTerm2’s Kitty image protocol implementation has an arbitrary command execution vulnerability in the file transmit error response path.
  • Three independent issues combine into a single exploit chain: (1) the APC handler lacks the trust check present in OSC handlers, (2) the Kitty file transmit error path preserves literal newlines from NSError.localizedDescription, and (3) the response is unconditionally written to PTY stdin.
  • It has been revealed that when the VT100 parser receives an APC sequence, it calls executeAPC:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iTerm2’s Kitty image protocol implementation has an arbitrary command execution vulnerability in the file transmit error response path. An APC escape sequence embedded in any file is consumed by the VT100 parser and does not appear in the cat output itself, but the Kitty file transmit error response preserves literal newlines from a crafted file path and writes them to PTY stdin — the shell interprets these newlines as command separators, resulting in arbitrary command execution. This is a logic bug — no memory corruption or race condition required — and is 100% reproducible. It works on a default iTerm2 installation with no configuration changes, and triggers on all shells including bash, zsh, and fish.

Three independent issues combine into a single exploit chain: (1) the APC handler lacks the trust check present in OSC handlers, (2) the Kitty file transmit error path preserves literal newlines from NSError.localizedDescription, and (3) the response is unconditionally written to PTY stdin.

It has been revealed that when the VT100 parser receives an APC sequence, it calls executeAPC:. At [A], it checks for tmux mode — if active, it returns early. At [B], it checks only whether the string starts with “G”, and at [C] creates a Kitty image command and passes it to the delegate. Compared to OSC sequence handling, the terminalIsTrusted check is completely absent. Any APC that reaches the VT100 parser is unconditionally executed regardless of source.

Recent findings suggest that no trust check exists in the delegate chain either. At [A], the command is passed directly to kittyImageController.

When the Kitty image controller receives a t=f (file transmit) command, it decodes the base64 payload and uses it as a file path. At [A], URL.resourceValues() checks whether the file exists — if it doesn’t, an exception is thrown. At [B], the filenameIsSafe() blocklist check exists, but this code is only reachable after resourceValues() succeeds, so it never executes for non-existent files. At [C], the catch block embeds error.localizedDescription directly into the error message. macOS’s NSError.localizedDescription preserves literal newlines (0x0A) in filenames without escaping them.

The response containing the error message is written to PTY stdin. At [A], the default verbosity .normal always sends the response — it is sent regardless of whether it is an error. At [B], the response is wrapped in APC format (ESC_G...ESC\) and passed to the delegate.

Sources indicate that at the end of the delegate chain, [A] the response data is written to the PTY via screenSendReportData:. This function sends data through the same path as keyboard input, so the shell interprets this data as if the user typed it.

Sources indicate that the developer confirmed and fixed the vulnerability across two commits. Adding a terminalIsTrusted check to the APC handler would not have protected default installations — terminalIsTrusted is simply the inverse of the advanced setting “Disable potentially insecure escape sequences,” which is off by default (the terminal is trusted by default). The response sanitization is what closes the hole for everyone.

In a recent development, the first fix adds sanitizedResponseMessage(_:) to KittyImageController.swift. It replaces every C0 control character (0x00–0x1F, including ESC, CR, LF) and DEL (0x7F) with a space before the response is framed and sent. The error payload in respondToTransmit() and respondToDisplay() is passed through this sanitizer. a53b1bc.

The follow-up commit extracts a shared sanitizer stringByReplacingControlCharactersWithSpace on NSString, extending coverage to C1 characters (0x80–0x9F) while preserving Unicode format characters (Cf) such as ZWJ and bidi marks. It replaces the per-file sanitizer and is applied to three report paths: Kitty image, Kitty drag-and-drop (OSC 72), and title reporting. 2a63835.

The Kitty drag-and-drop sanitizer was changed from stripping only CR/LF to stripping all control characters, and the title report sanitizer was hardened the same way.

The attack vector is embedding APC escape sequence bytes into a malicious file. When the entire file content is output to the terminal (e.g., via cat), the raw bytes are delivered to the terminal and processed by the VT100 parser. This works on all shells — bash, zsh, fish, etc. — the shell type is irrelevant.

Industry observers note that the APC sequence (starting with ESC _, ending with ESC \) is consumed by iTerm2’s VT100 parser and is invisible in the cat output — the file appears to be a normal document. However, when the exploit triggers, the error response injected into PTY stdin produces visible garbled shell errors on the terminal. The injected command executes between these garbled lines, so the command execution itself is visible to the user. Concealment of this output was not explored in this research.

The core of the attack relies on two facts: macOS NSError.localizedDescription preserves literal newlines in filenames, and the error message uses curly quotes instead of ASCII double-quotes.

Why ASCII double-quotes are not used: If ASCII " is included in the file path, it appears as-is in the error message. When delivered to the shell via PTY, bash enters double-quote mode upon encountering ", and newlines no longer act as command separators. macOS’s NSError.localizedDescription uses Unicode curly quotes (“, ”), which are not special characters in bash and do not trigger quote mode.

The file path set by the attacker (before base64 encoding):.

APC bytes can be embedded in any file type — .md, .txt, .log, .csv, configuration files, source code, etc. The only requirement is that the file content is output to the terminal via cat. The following example uses a README.md, but any file that a user might cat is a valid vector. The APC itself is invisible in cat output (consumed by the VT100 parser), but the error response injected into PTY stdin appears as garbled shell errors alongside the executed command.

Fund browser-grade certificate checking for every TLS client

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (539 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rustls

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Non-browser applications have historically relied on a slowly changing set of trust roots maintained by the operating system or platform vendors.
  • The October 2026 eMudhra incident revealed the cost.
  • According to recent reports, upki ships these signals as a compact local cache that's updated automatically, independently of applications, so every TLS stack on a machine can share one copy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Non-browser applications have historically relied on a slowly changing set of trust roots maintained by the operating system or platform vendors. These trust roots are often based on browser root programs, but lack the data that allow browsers to make fine-grained trust decisions: revocation data for end entities, intermediates and roots (like CRLite and OneCRL), distrust dates and Certificate Transparency policy.

The October 2026 eMudhra incident revealed the cost. Browsers blocked the affected intermediates promptly, while other clients were unable to restrict only the affected intermediates. Instead, they had to wait for platform trust store updates to remove the parent root certificates and spent significant time and effort to mitigate the impact on their applications across different platforms and environments.

According to recent reports, upki ships these signals as a compact local cache that's updated automatically, independently of applications, so every TLS stack on a machine can share one copy. Its checks only ever narrow what a client accepts: they never make it trust a certificate it would otherwise reject.

Sources indicate that sponsorships are annual and pay for maintainer time on the roadmap and on ongoing maintenance. We don't sell individual features; priorities are open for discussion with sponsors.

For more information, contact Dirkjan Ochtman.

Sponsors help set priorities through quarterly roadmap calls.

Clients outside the browser accept revoked end-entity certificates.

upki syncs compact CRLite filters several times a day and checks revocation offline.

When root programs distrust a CA or intermediate, other clients keep trusting it until a trust store package revision arrives, as the eMudhra incident revealed.

upki will ship OneCRL data, so distrust takes effect at the next cache revision.

Industry observers note that post-quantum signatures would add kilobytes to every TLS handshake. Merkle Tree Certificates can bring down the costs, but clients need landmarks delivered ahead of time to minimize handshake overhead.

upki will distribute landmarks alongside its other data.

Recent findings suggest that clients that don't enforce Certificate Transparency accept certificates that were never publicly logged, so misissuance can go unnoticed. Clients also don't benefit from certificate transparency logs blocking compromised/distrusted roots from obtaining proof of inclusion.

upki will deliver and maintain an up-to-date log list and policy inputs, so applications don't have to configure logs manually.

Servers that send an incomplete certificate chain work in browsers but fail verification in other clients.

upki will ship the known intermediate certificates, so clients can complete the chain as browsers do, without expensive network fetching.

Root changes, including private PKI roots, reach machines through OS packages or configuration management, which can be slow and uneven across a fleet.

upki's sync mechanism could distribute root sets to every machine.

The checks only protect applications whose TLS stack uses upki.

upki could gain native support in OpenSSL upstream, GnuTLS, NSS or in language runtimes.

Every check depends on data that's refreshed several times a day, on upstream sources and formats that keep changing, and on prompt fixes when security problems come up.

Sponsorship pays for releases, security response, dependency updates, keeping the data pipeline running and in step with upstream changes, supporting distribution packagers and maintaining C2SP specifications.

upki lives in the rustls organization on GitHub and is dual-licensed under Apache-2.0 and MIT.

It has been revealed that MLX is Apple's framework for local AI, especially optimized for Apple Silicon. We are major MLX supporters since it was the Christmas present from Awni and Angelos in 2023, and proud that Hugging Face is the Hub where people find MLX models and contribute their own. Usage of open, local AI is accelerating, and we believe in a healthy ecosystem where people can find the tools that work for them.

Stability, and hopefully faster development! Graduating from a side job to a fully maintained and funded project will allow Jun to better guide the contributors and build for the long-term. oMLX stays Apache 2.0, and Jun keeps leading it as before.

In a recent development, our end goal is to unblock the community to run local AI in any shape or form, and provide the tools and building blocks to make that happen. We expect oMLX to serve as a testbed for new ideas, while leveraging the foundational work of the dependencies it already relies upon, such as mlx-lm or mlx-vlm. We believe that strong modeling and inference libraries help the community, so we'd love to upstream work to wherever it makes sense. We have been collaborating with many projects mlx-lm, mlx-vlm, LMStudio, and we hope we can strengthen the relationship with Cheng, Prince, Yagil, and their teams to better serve the community together.

It has been revealed that concretely, one focus area is the quick transition from a transformers model definition to a reference MLX implementation that can be consumed by different engines, so each one can focus on the unique features they provide. The transformers library has become the reference for ML model definitions, we want to streamline the process to make newly introduced transformers models run on MLX.

We are incredibly excited about the future.

Microsoft brings serverless PostgreSQL into Fabric to bridge transactions and analytics

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (999 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • HorizonDB preview follows rivals' moves, with analysts warning tighter integration could make an eventual exit harder.
  • Microsoft has brought its HorizonDB PostgreSQL service into public preview in Fabric, aiming to bring transactional and analytical workloads closer together.
  • The corporation says applications can submit queries through a single PostgreSQL endpoint, with transactional and analytical work handled by the appropriate engines.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

HorizonDB preview follows rivals' moves, with analysts warning tighter integration could make an eventual exit harder.

Microsoft has brought its HorizonDB PostgreSQL service into public preview in Fabric, aiming to bring transactional and analytical workloads closer together.

The corporation says applications can submit queries through a single PostgreSQL endpoint, with transactional and analytical work handled by the appropriate engines.

Analysts mentioned the move follows similar efforts by Databricks and Snowflake to combine operational databases with analytics. But tighter integration with Microsoft's stack could make applications harder to move elsewhere.

Sources indicate that fabric HorizonDB joins SQL database and Cosmos DB in Microsoft's Fabric database portfolio. "By bringing operational databases, analytics, and AI together on a unified, governed platform, developers can build intelligent applications with less data movement and complexity. Fabric HorizonDB will also serve as the PostgreSQL backend for Fabric apps," Microsoft noted.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft first unveiled Azure HorizonDB in preview in November 2025 and made it generally available last week. It competes with other cloud database services and distributed systems such as CockroachDB and YugabyteDB, both of which support PostgreSQL's wire protocol.

At the time, it remarked HorizonDB would offer "massive read scale without the need to replicate the database between instances.".

Speaking to The Register last week, Shireesh Thota, veep of Azure databases and Fabric applications, noted that bringing the system into Fabric – its platform for data lakes, data warehouses, and analytics debuted in 2023 – would connect operational data in HorizonDB with analytical data in OneLake, Fabric's unified data lake.

"Once the data hits the OneLake storage, you can have analytical engines that take advantage of it. In HorizonDB, the PostgreSQL query engine can talk to the distributed query engine that we use in our Fabric data warehouse. We're fusing these query engines, thereby enabling the developers to submit a query that has pieces of the query that can work on OLTP and pieces of the query that can work on OLAP," he mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that "The application need not worry about two endpoints, or about consistency of data and all that complexity. They can just talk to HorizonDB as a Fabric endpoint, and they can submit all these queries. We are basically operationalizing in OneLake.".

Operational data remains in HorizonDB's database storage, while mirroring maintains an analytical copy in OneLake, introduced in 2023, which replicates a snapshot of the external database to OneLake in Delta Parquet tables and keeps the replica synced in "near real time.".

Sources indicate that thota remarked the process would not affect the transactional system. "Our core goal is to never impact OLTP workload while we are doing this, and we succeed [by] reading off the log as an additional replica to do this mirroring," he said.

But the overall blueprint of putting serverless PostgreSQL OLTP in an analytics platform, bringing it close to OLAP systems, is one some vendors are already executing to meet the demands of new AI agent-led workloads.

Adam Ronthal, research veep in Gartner's Data and Analytics Group, said: "The addition of Microsoft Fabric HorizonDB follows the 2025 acquisitions of PostgreSQL vendors by Databricks – Neon – and Snowflake – Crunchy. It delivers a high-performance, serverless operational RDBMS that is tightly coupled with Microsoft's lakehouse offering and well-suited to the ephemeral demands of AI agents.

In a recent development, "Competing directly with AWS Aurora and Google Cloud's AlloyDB, HorizonDB acts as a foundational serving layer for the next generation of AI- and analytics-infused applications. For organizations aligned with Azure and Fabric, it provides an industry-standard PostgreSQL foundation for AI development.".

Andrew Snodgrass, research vice president of analyst company Directions on Microsoft, said the announcement of HorizonDB in Fabric was a "surprise," although "a watered-down version" compared to the version of the serverless database that became generally available on Azure last week. "It joins (document database) CosmosDB in Fabric and SQL database (based on the SQL Server engine) in Fabric. It highlights that Microsoft is still focused on making Fabric the data hub of their universe.".

According to recent reports, horizonDB – both in Azure and Fabric – is a PostgreSQL service which Microsoft states has 100 percent compatibility with the open source system that has enjoyed a meteoric rise over the last decade. The support for PostgreSQL has led some to question the software giant's commitment to its own proprietary OLTP system, SQL Server.

Thota pointed out that the SQL database, based on the SQL Server engine, is already available in Fabric. Microsoft is also evaluating similar integration for that service, although he gave no timetable. "We are just beginning this journey, and most of the innovation is neutral to PostgreSQL and SQL. Some of it would be particular to how the individual query engine fuses with the analytical query engine. PostgreSQL does it slightly differently than SQL, but the idea is that most of the work is neutral. We are evaluating that work as well. I don't have timelines for that, but it is certainly in our thinking," he said.

Recent findings suggest that nonetheless, Holger Mueller, principal analyst at Constellation Research, said it was good to see Microsoft go all in on support of open source. "In general, it is an acknowledgement that they cannot win the battle for the SQL database with SQL Server – as it is as proprietary as the leader Oracle – and now they bank on the openness of PostgreSQL as another approach," he said.

However, using HorizonDB integrated into the Fabric/Azure stack may create so many dependencies with Microsoft's technology that lock-in to the vendor will remain a risk. "The primary concerns of open source – scale and support – have been eliminated by Microsoft's commitment and by now track record... the challenges are the embeddings of HorizonDB into the bigger Microsoft stack – which will make portability hard again. But every vendor wants and provides stickiness – clothed in ease of use and lower TCO," Mueller noted. ®.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs.
  • Industry observers note that running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a major part of that.
  • And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

Industry observers note that running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a major part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

A recent example of what local AI can feel like:.

This is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU.

GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so users can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

We want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

According to recent reports, GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:.

Industry observers note that we suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

No extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

That is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:.

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

Industry observers note that the model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

For models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:.

transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

In a recent development, our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

Industry observers note that the llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

In a recent development, transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

When GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

It has been revealed that llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:.

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):.

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

In a recent development, transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for fresh architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

It has been revealed that that opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

We also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

Our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

Recent findings suggest that A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

In a recent development, the kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

Industry observers note that the first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

Industry observers note that to show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

Sources indicate that faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):.

Recent findings suggest that these changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

The initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:.

If you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an issue with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.

We would like to thank Arthur Zucker for initiating this work and reviewing all of my PRs, and Cyril Vallez for the generate PRs. We are grateful to Sayak Paul, the llama.cpp team, and Bertrand Chevalier for their help integrating the kernels. We also thank Aritra Roy Gosthipaty and Pedro Cuenca for reviewing this blog post, and Lysandre Debut for overseeing the project.

InfoQ Homepage News Java News Roundup: Java4Shell, Oracle CSPUs, OpenJDK, Azul Payara, BellSoft, Helidon, LangChain4j.

Nov 23, 2026 7 min read.

This week's Java roundup for November 16th, 2026, features news highlighting: the Java4Shell RCE vulnerability; Oracle CSPUs; Lazy Constants targeted for JDK 28; the November 2026 edition of Azul Payara; point releases of Java Operator SDK, LangChain4j and Micrometer; maintenance releases of Liberica JDK and Helidon; and second release candidates of Hibernate Reactive.

It has been revealed that oracle has released versions 27.0.1.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 17.0.21.0.3, 11.0.33.0.3 and 8u511b3 of the JDK as part of their quarterly Critical Security Patch Patch Advisory for November 2026. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes for version 27.0.1.0.3, version 25.0.5.0.3, version 21.0.13.0.3, version 17.0.21.0.3, version 11.0.33.0.3 and version 8u511 b33.

JEP 547, Lazy Constants (Fourth Preview), has been elevated from Proposed to Target to Targeted for JDK 28. This JEP proposes a fourth preview, with no changes, after three rounds of preview delivered in the upcoming release of JDK 27 and JDK 26 through JDK 25. Formerly known as Stable Values and Computed Constants, this feature introduces the concept of computed constants, defined as immutable value holders that are initialized at most once. This offers the performance and safety benefits of final fields, while offering greater flexibility as to the timing of initialization. The name change from Stable Values to Lazy Constants with the release of JDK 26, better captures the intent of a high-level use case.

Sources indicate that JEP 548, Vector API (Thirteenth Incubator), has been elevated from its JEP Draft 8397768 to Candidate status. This JEP proposes a thirteenth incubation with one notable change, after twelve rounds of incubation delivered in JDK 16 through JDK 27. This feature introduces an API to "express vector computations that reliably compile at runtime to optimal vector instructions on supported CPU architectures, thus achieving performance superior to equivalent scalar computations." This JEP adds support for Vector vectors, whose lanes hold 16-bit floating-point numbers in the IEEE 754 binary16 format. The Vector API will continue to incubate until the necessary features of Project Valhalla become available as preview features. At that time, the Vector API team will adapt the Vector API and its implementation to use them, and will promote the Vector API from Incubation to Preview.

Build 25 of the JDK 28 early-access builds was made available this past week featuring updates from Build 24 that include fixes for various problems. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

For JDK 28, developers are encouraged to report bugs via the Java Bug Database.

A upcoming Remote Code Execution (RCE) vulnerability, known as Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), affects versions 27.0.1.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 17.0.21.0.3 and 8u511b33-perf of Oracle Java SE, versions 21.0.13.0.3 and 17.0.21.0.3 of Oracle GraalVM for JDK, and Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition: 21.3.20.0.3. As described in the CVE documentation:.

Industry observers note that [This] difficult to exploit vulnerability allows [an] unauthenticated attacker with network access via multiple protocols to compromise Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition. Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in takeover of Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition. Note: This vulnerability can only be exploited by supplying data to APIs in the specified Component without using Untrusted Java Web Start applications or Untrusted Java applets, such as through a web service.

Industry observers note that organizations and projects that have addressed this CVE include: BellSoft, Azul, JetBrains, GraalVM, Quarkus and WildFly. InfoQ will follow up with a more detailed news story.

It was a busy week over at Spring as the various teams have delivered GA releases that include: Spring Boot, Spring Framework, Spring Security, Spring Session, Spring Integration, Spring HATEOAS, Spring Modulith, Spring AI, Spring AMQP, Spring for Apache Kafka and Spring LDAP.

The Spring team has also resolved a total of 90 CVEs spanning multiple projects. InfoQ will follow up with a more detailed news story.

Industry observers note that the release of Azul Payara 7.6.0, the November 2026 edition, includes Community Edition 7.2026.11, Enterprise Edition 6.44.0 and Enterprise Edition 5.93.0. Along with bug fixes and component upgrades, all three editions deliver resolutions to five CVEs, two of which are related to Azul Payara:.

Further details on this release may be found in the release notes and the Azul Payara security advisories page.

The second release candidates of Hibernate Reactive 5.1.0 and 5.0.0 ship with one single bug fix from the first release candidates, in which use of the Jakarta Persistence @TableGenerator annotation could cause a deadlock when a session holding the lock on the row of the generator table needed a upcoming block of IDs.

Version 5.0.0.CR2 will be the last release candidate. With the GA release of version 5.0.0.Final, it will be declared as end-of-life and focus will be on version 5.1.0.

More details on these releases may be found in the release notes for version 5.1.0.CR2 and version 5.0.0.CR2.

The release of Java Operator SDK 5.7.0 provides bug fixes, dependency upgrades and new features such as: the ability to enable virtual threads via construction in the Operator class or the josdk.use-virtual-threads property; and a new keepAlive() method, defined in the Operator class that starts a non-daemon thread to keep the JVM running until the operator is shut down. Version 5.7 is now built on Fabric8 Kubernetes Client 8.0. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

Concurrent with Oracle's Critical Security Patch Update (CSPU) for November 2026, BellSoft has released CSPU patches for versions 27.0.1.1 25.0.5.1, 21.0.13.1, 17.0.21.1, 11.0.33.1, 8u514 7u523 and 6u523 of Liberica JDK, their downstream distribution of OpenJDK, to address this list of CVEs. This release also includes a patch for the aforementioned Java4Shell Remote Code Execution vulnerability.

With an overall total of 111 fixes and backports, BellSoft states they have participated in eliminating 21 issues in all releases.

The release of Helidon 27.0.2 delivers bug fixes and one notable change in which the default limit of decoded-input (strings, byte arrays, JSON, forms, and buffered multipart parts) for in-memory entity conversations has been increased to 1 mebibyte (MiB). More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

This release also aligns with the Oracle Critical Patch Updates for November 2026 and includes the Helidon 4.x and 3.x release trains as described in this blog post.

In a recent development, the formal release (along with the thirty-fourth beta release) of LangChain4j 1.24.0 ships with bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: new DecisionSchedulerPlanner and DecisionModels classes to serve as a decision model-based agentic pattern; and support for resuming suspended agentic systems in the AgentMonitor class. Further details on this release, including breaking changes, may be found in the release notes.

It has been revealed that after two milestones and two releases candidates, the GA release of Micrometer Metrics 1.18.0 provides bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and latest features such as: an optimization of the PrometheusMeterRegistry and MicrometerCollector classes for collecting data snapshots; and a new RowState inner class, defined in the MultiGauge class, that eliminates the need to remove and re-register an instance of the existing Row inner class. More details on this release, including deprecations, may be found in the release notes.

Similarly, the GA release of Micrometer Tracing 1.8.0 delivers bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: a simplification of baggage handles and lookups by directly storing the name of the handle and its metadata by eliminating use of the CompositeBaggage and Java AtomicReference classes; and a refactor of the BaggageTextMapPropagator class for improved baggage propagation. Further details on this release, including deprecations, may be found in the release notes.

  • The key is a relationship among the four powers of two in this identity:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this post introduces a fresh algorithm for extracting hexadecimal digits of \(\pi\) without computing the preceding digits. It beats the standard term-by-term evaluations of Bailey–Borwein–Plouffe (BBP), Bellard, and Huvent on operation count. Even against Huvent’s eight-term formula, the savings at large offsets are about 61% fewer divisions and 38% fewer full modular exponentiations.

The key is a relationship among the four powers of two in this identity:.

The common denominator \(M=2k+1\) means we can add four remainders and divide once. The surprise is that we don’t have to compute those remainders independently either. As we will see, the gaps between them stay small multiples of \(k\) plus constants, so one starting power and the step \(2^k\bmod M\) let us reach the others by multiplication.

Recent findings suggest that even better, working modulo \(3M\) lets the same two exponentiations serve both \(M\) and \(3M\). Eight powers of two over two different denominators can share two full exponentiations and a single division. For every million hexadecimal places skipped, that saves about a million full exponentiations compared with Huvent, before any machine-specific optimization enters into it.

It has been revealed that to see where the savings come from, recall the BBP trick. To skip \(n\) hex digits, shift \(\pi\) left by \(d=4n\) bits and take the fractional part. For a term \(2^E/N\) with \(E\ge 0\), we only need \((2^E\bmod N)/N\) because the difference is an integer which doesn’t contribute to the fractional part. So even at \(d=4{,}000{,}000\) we never have to construct a four-million-bit numerator. The terms with negative exponents still count; they decay geometrically, so we can sum their tails directly, keeping enough guard bits to settle the last digit we want.

Last time, I counted the work by counting fractions. Bellard’s formula advances 10 bits for every seven fractions; Huvent’s formula advances 12 bits for every eight. After finding Huvent’s formula independently, I’ve feverishly tried to find one with a better ratio, without success. So I looked toward ways of optimizing existing series.

According to recent reports, one clue tipped me off. There’s a choice hiding in the last step of Bellard’s derivation. He has one sum in powers of \(1/4\) and another in powers of \(1/1024\). Since \(4^5=1024\), splitting the first sum into five progressions lets him write both sums in powers of \(1/1024\). What if, instead of lining up the powers, we lined up the denominators?

Lining up denominators seemed hard with the many-term series of Bellard and Huvent. One good place I found to try this is a series Euler wrote down in 1779. Craig-Wood used it to extract hexadecimal digits1. In the original notation there are six rows:.

Takahashi writes this straightforwardly as two sums:.

Notice what we’re dividing by. Since \(4m+2=2(2m+1)\), we can halve the numerator of the middle fraction and leave \(2m+1\) in the denominator. As \(m\) runs over the nonnegative integers, \(2m+1\) gives every positive odd integer. The other two progressions, \(4m+1\) and \(4m+3\), split that same list between them. So each odd denominator appears twice in each sum.

For example, consider the denominator 13. The first progression hits it at \(m=3\); the middle one hits it at \(m=6\), where the original denominator was 26. That’s two contributions from the sum in powers of \(1/64\) and two from the sum in powers of \(1/1024\). The powers are different, but all four numerators can be added before we divide by 13. We can collect terms this way for every odd denominator.

It has been revealed that to derive the boxed formula directly, we can start with a multiplication of Gaussian integers: \((3-i)^2(7-i)=50(1-i)\). Taking complex arguments gives Hutton’s arctangent identity from the 18th century:.

It has been revealed that bellard lists this identity as equation (7). His logarithm trick works on both angles: \(1-(1+i)/4=(3-i)/4\), and \(1-(1+i)/8=(7-i)/8\). So if we put.

Sources indicate that then \(I_2=\arctan(1/3)\), \(I_3=\arctan(1/7)\), and we want \(\pi=8I_2+4I_3\). Every time \(j\) goes up by four, \((1+i)^j/2^{uj}\) is multiplied by \(-4/2^{4u}\). That’s \(-1/64\) in the first sum and \(-1/1024\) in the second.

For an odd denominator \(N=2k+1\), the two contributions in each logarithm come from \(j=N\) and \(j=2N\). All further doublings give multiples of four, where \((1+i)^j\) is real and contributes nothing. At \(j=N\) the imaginary part of \((1+i)^N\) is \((-1)^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}2^k\); at \(j=2N\) we’re looking at \((2i)^N=(-1)^k 2^N i\). At \(j=N\), the first logarithm multiplies the imaginary part by \(8/2^{2(2k+1)}\), giving the numerator term \((-1)^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}2^{1-3k}\). Collect the other three contributions in the same way and we have the boxed formula.

After the shift by \(d\), that is, multiplying the sum by \(2^d\), the four exponents, in the order we wrote them, are.

According to recent reports, call a power active if its exponent is nonnegative. The slowest-decaying exponent is \(E_1\), which stays nonnegative up to \(k=\lfloor(d+1)/3\rfloor\). That’s about \(d/3\) odd denominators, and we divide just once for each one. Even the largest modulus is only \(2d/3+O(1)\), compared with about \(d\) for Bellard or Huvent, and \(2d\) for the original BBP formula.

As for the remainders \(r_j=2^{E_j}\bmod N\), notice that the middle two exponents differ by \(k\). If we already have \(r_3\) and \(x=2^k\bmod N\), then \(r_2\) is just \(xr_3\bmod N\). In fact, we can step from the smallest exponent up to the largest:.

Sources indicate that start at the smallest active power. We pay for one full exponentiation to get it and one to get \(x\); the rest are a handful of multiplications. Past \(k\approx d/5\) only \(E_1\) is active, so don’t bother computing \(x\).2 That’s two exponentiations for the first \(d/5\) denominators and one for the remaining \(d/3-d/5\), or about \(8d/15\) altogether.

There’s one more thing we can do with 13. Suppose we’re going to compute remainders modulo 39 anyway. A remainder modulo 39 is good modulo 13 too, and \(A/13+B/39=(3A+B)/39\), so we only need a single division by 39.

To avoid counting a denominator twice, we start a pair only at an odd \(M\) that isn’t divisible by three. If \(3M\) is in range, we handle it together with \(M\); otherwise we handle \(M\) alone. So 39 gets handled with 13, and we don’t also pair 39 with 117. Multiples of nine, like 117, get their own turn.

It has been revealed that the two numerators can share the exponentiations, too. The index for \(M=2k+1\) is \(k\); for \(3M\) it’s \(3k+1\). For 13 and 39 those indices are 6 and 19: once we have \(2^6\bmod 39\), we get \(2^{19}\bmod 39\) just by cubing and doubling. In general, all eight exponents have the same \(d\), so their differences are small multiples of \(k\) plus constants. We compute just two powers modulo \(3M\): the smallest active power across the pair and the step \(2^k\). Multiplication gives us the rest. The largest exponent for \(3M\) is \(d-2-9k\), so it drops out near \(k=d/9\), before \(M\) stops needing the step near \(k=d/5\). Whenever there’s a partner, \(M\) would already need two exponentiations on its own.

Industry observers note that in any nine consecutive odd denominators, three are divisible by three. One of those is divisible by nine and keeps its own turn, while the other two are absorbed into their smaller partners. That leaves seven trips through the loop instead of nine, both where we need one exponentiation and where we need two. Multiplying the counts above by \(7/9\) gives about \(7d/27\) divisions and \(56d/135\) full exponentiations, compared to \(2d/3\) of each for Huvent.

Here is how the formulas compare in bits of offset per operation:.

Industry observers note that I implemented both the algorithm of this post and Huvent using AVX-512 IFMA. Here’s how long each took to extract 12 hex digits on my computer.

These are median times except at a trillion digits, where I timed each method once. The percentages use unrounded times: 62.3% faster in the last row means 38.4% less elapsed time.

Sources indicate that returning to the pair 13 and 39, while 39 is active, I never reduce modulo 13: changing the numerator for 13 by a multiple of 13 changes its tripled contribution by a multiple of 39. So I do all the squaring and multiplying modulo 39. Since 39 is odd, I can compute its inverse modulo a power of two once and reuse it for every Montgomery multiplication in the pair. I triple the numerator for 13, add the one for 39, and convert back from Montgomery form just once for the final division.

According to recent reports, there’s a nice trick inside each exponentiation, too. Suppose a Montgomery reduction leaves \(-14\) modulo 39. Normally I’d add 39 to get 25. But if I’m going to square it next, 14 is just as good: \(14^2\equiv25^2\pmod{39}\). Even if the current exponent bit calls for doubling first, the next square still erases the sign. So for all but the last bit, I use vector absolute values instead of correcting the sign. On the last bit I do the usual reduction, since the numerator needs the actual residue rather than its negative. That change made the exponentiation loop about 8% faster on Zen 5.

In a recent development, each vector lane handles a different odd modulus. I batch moduli with the same set of active powers so that one lane doesn’t sit idle while another steps through three extra residues. The hardware multiplies 52-bit inputs, so the largest modulus matters: ours is about \(2d/3\), compared with \(d\) for Huvent. That lets us reach about 50% farther into \(\pi\) before we need wider arithmetic.

I originally went looking for a series with fewer fractions per bit. If you evaluate every fraction separately, Euler’s series actually needs more fractions per bit than Huvent’s, so it has been easy to pass over. Sharing the modular arithmetic across common and paired denominators is what makes it faster, and I suspect similar tricks apply to other BBP-type series.

His implementation evaluates 21 fractions separately for every 30 bits of offset. ↩︎.

Recent findings suggest that there’s a way to thin out the far end of the loop even more. At \(j=4m+3\), the real and imaginary parts of \((1+i)^j\) are opposites. Add the real part of each logarithm and the two slow powers cancel for \(N\equiv3\pmod4\). We still have to subtract the real logarithms we added, using series for \(\log(1+2^{-2})\), \(\log(1+2^{-3})\), and \(\log(1-2^{-4})\). That leaves half as many moduli above \(d/2\), at the cost of more streams of powers to juggle below it. ↩︎.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meanwhile, Google's homepage demo leaves a familiar button out of the picture.

Microsoft is updating search in its Microsoft 365 Copilot app for customers without a Copilot license, with a toggle to restore the classic interface. Google, meanwhile, is giving AI searches more prominence on its homepage, where the familiar Search button is absent from a newly demonstrated layout.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft's change is rolling out now and will hit Deferred Release by mid-January 2027. It will impact consumers with a Microsoft 365 license who do not have a Copilot license and "provides modern search controls to help users find, refine, and navigate search results more easily.".

It has been revealed that it's enabled by default, which is a shame since administrators would likely prefer an opt-in rather than opt-out approach, and owners can switch back to the "classic search experience" via a toggle on the search results page. Microsoft has not specified how long this toggle will remain available. Its separate Copilot Search experience had a fallback toggle scheduled for removal 60 days after general availability.

"With the updated search experience, people can continue to find files using keywords, use modern search controls to refine and navigate results, and search supported connected third-party content when their organization has configured connected sources," Microsoft mentioned.

In a recent development, the results will still only display content to which people have permission. Microsoft advises administrators to brief users and help desks on the changed interface and the option to switch back.

Microsoft's search tweaks arrive as the future of the Google Search button on Google's desktop homepage looks uncertain.

In a recent development, in a post, Google VP of Product Robby Stein described a collapsible sidebar that lists consumers' recent AI conversations, pushing AI deeper into the search experience. Stein called it "a much simpler way to pick up where you left off," and said it would help customers "easily find & jump back into your recent AI searches.".

However, something else was obvious in Stein's post: the Google Search button was not present.

Stein explained in August that Google had performed a "small test on desktop to help people find latest things they can do with Search." Part of that test was the removal of the Google Search button.

Industry observers note that owners can still submit queries by pressing Enter. Stein remarked the test would have "no impact to how the core search works.".

According to recent reports, the sidebar rollout doesn't itself confirm the Search button's permanent retirement. For now, its absence from Stein's demonstration is another sign of which features Google wants users to notice. ®.

Breaking: How UK AISI and EvalEval Are Making Benchmark Results Reproducible

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.
  • In a recent development, AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema.
  • As AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

In a recent development, AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

As AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

This builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

Transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this latest phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:.

In a recent development, these results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve shows the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

When results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

According to recent reports, the EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

The coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Sources indicate that the UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Industry observers note that once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Recent findings suggest that reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.
