Lua for data representation

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1124 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Citrons

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • my major advocacy is that lua is a very good general purpose language.
  • In a recent development, lua’s syntax provides many niceties.
  • here is a function that for any string, creates the correct multiline string to represent it:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

my major advocacy is that lua is a very good general purpose language. this is not an opinion shared by all. lua’s major design goal was extending and embedding into existing programs. I think the simplicity and flexibility in design persued towards the end of that goal extends to make lua a very good language in general. that noted, it does its job quite well as an embedding language, and one of its more interesting use cases (and actually, one of its oldest use cases) is as a data or configuration format.

In a recent development, lua’s syntax provides many niceties. for instance, lua has an infinite family of multiline strings: the most basic one starts with [[ and ends with ]]. however, any amount of equal signs can be put between the two square brackets: print([======[hello, world]======]). the only way to close a [===[ is with an accompanying ]===], not with a ]] or a ]==], or a ]====].

here is a function that for any string, creates the correct multiline string to represent it:.

local function stringize(str) local equal_signs = "" for e in str:gmatch("](=*)]") do if #e >= #equal_signs then equal_signs = e .. "=" end end return ("[%s[%s]%s]"):format(equal_signs, str, equal_signs) end of course, you can just use string.format with %q, but multiline strings usually provide nicer looking and more compact results. these strings are very good for representing lua code as strings in other lua code.

According to recent reports, anyway, download this file. if you want to consume massive amounts of memory and possibly crash your computer, run it in cpython. if you want to see “hello, world” printed 5 million times, run it in lua. lua’s parser is designed to handle massive files with stride, which is fairly unique and quite necessary if lua is to be used for this purpose.

design and implementation choices like these come together to suit lua for this purpose. I’ve seen 3 main styles of using lua code to represent data or configuration. I think lua manages to accomodate each of them well, and each have their appropriate use.

According to recent reports, chunks are much like function bodies. they have return values. so, one thing that one can do is just return a massive table from a lua program.

return { foo = "bar", list = {1, 2, 3}, rule_of_thirds = true, } if you’re using this style, you can omit the return and then prepend it when you load the lua files. this makes any trailing statements syntactically invalid because the return statement must be the last statement in the block. keep in mind, though, that this does not prevent arbitrary code because function literals can be used instead.

Recent findings suggest that return (function() arbitrary_code() end)() trying to strip out function literals to make this technique safer is fraught and defeats the general elegance of this technique. one can fairly readily use JSON instead.

what is often missed about lua is that it’s subtly full of metaprogrammability. for instance, lua globals are just stored in a table, and which table is used can be controlled by the code itself. this table is known as the “environment”. an environment may be passed to load as an argument. the way this can be used is that you can load a chunk with an empty environment and then capture the values it sets as globals.

-- config.lua foo = "bar" list = {1, 2, 3} rule_of_thirds = true then, you can get a table with all the configuration as simply as this:.

local config = {} assert(loadfile("config.lua", "t", config))().

lua has a bit of sugar that allows you to shed the parenthesis on function calls to make them look cleaner. an imperative style is a very suitable means to represent data in lua, and it’s very powerful.

It has been revealed that path "/path/to/things" config { foo = "bar", list = {1, 2, 3}, rule_of_thirds = true, } lipsum [[ Voluptatibus laudantium et omnis ut debitis. Similique omnis molestias consequuntur. Praesentium corporis omnis nihil et quidem dolore. Veritatis fugiat eaque corporis eligendi officiis praesentium. Libero quo vero temporibus impedit sit inventore assumenda ]] programming in lua provides a real world example of this.

It has been revealed that the major problem with using an entire programming language to represent data is that untrusted data can be readily crafted to be malicious. indeed, I would not use this technique for untrusted data. with that in mind, it is possible to solve or mitigate the potential vulnerabilities.

Industry observers note that the main technique for sandboxing lua is controlling the environment. when using lua for data representation, an empty enivronment is the most appropriate (or, an environment that only exposes data constructors). this prevents any I/O or access to the larger program’s state. preventing access to all standard library functions is safest. there are a few standard library functions that have consequences you might not expect.

In a recent development, another concern is denial of service. this is trickier to prevent. it’s fairly trivial to construct a lua chunk which does not return (while true do end). debug.sethook can mitigate this somewhat. even so, it’s probably possible to construct something that uses excessive amounts of memory. that said, denial of service is significantly less problematic than the vulnerabilities that are completely avoided by depriving the untrusted code of any standard library functions.

finally, make sure to reject lua bytecode. untrusted lua bytecode is not safe and may cause arbitrary nasal demons in the lua interpreter. load can accept both bytecode and lua source by default. however, passing "t" for the mode parameter prevents this.

Recent findings suggest that clearly, it’s silly to bring in the entire lua interpreter where you would just use JSON or INI. where this use case of lua shines is when you’re already using lua for a project (and then you already have this powerful data description language), or when you need something with a lot of power or flexibility.

these mini languages can be extended to arbitrary complexity and nuance. unlike JSON, you can add arbitrary type constructors, or anything at all. you can build any kind of language you want, and that’s how lua is designed to be used, and it’s actually approximately the story of how it was invented.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re anything like me, this will sound a little familiar. indeed, many have noted similar things about lisp and forth. both of those languages have very different approaches but reach the same conclusion of “inventing your own language”. I believe lua belongs in their pantheon.

python? js? ruby? what the hell are those? all I care about is LUA.

An AI coding agent, a browser, and a Mac tool found a financial firm's access key in under 6 minutes

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1083 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • No sophisticated malware or attack framework required.
  • A Romanian hacker, armed with only an open source coding agent, a Chrome browser, and a Mac, tried multiple ways to break into a financial services firm, ultimately found an access key - luckily, it was a decoy - and carried out an entire (almost) attack in under six minutes.
  • It’s a stark reminder that miscreants don’t need sophisticated malware - as in the Binance heist - or AI pen-testing tools like ARTEX to carry out intrusions into critical networks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

No sophisticated malware or attack framework required.

A Romanian hacker, armed with only an open source coding agent, a Chrome browser, and a Mac, tried multiple ways to break into a financial services firm, ultimately found an access key - luckily, it was a decoy - and carried out an entire (almost) attack in under six minutes.

It’s a stark reminder that miscreants don’t need sophisticated malware - as in the Binance heist - or AI pen-testing tools like ARTEX to carry out intrusions into critical networks. Open source coding agents, and specifically OpenCode in this case, also work just fine.

“What surprised me most was how little it took and the toolkit: a free coding agent, the curl that comes with every Mac and an ordinary Chrome, all from one laptop,” Jesta co-founder and CTO Lior Finkelshtein told The Register. “Until now I thought that we had more time until tools like OpenCode are used in offensive operations. This incident demonstrates us that it's already in use in the field, and we will probably see more of that in the future.”.

Jesta is a Tel Aviv-based security startup that builds defensive tools to detect and stop autonomous AI attacks. In a report shared exclusively with The Register, Finkelshtein documented an attempted intrusion targeting a major financial services company that’s also a Jesta customer - the security shop declined to say which one.

It has been revealed that jesta’s investigation into the incident determined that someone in Bucharest downloaded a free AI coding agent called OpenCode and pointed it at the financial services customer on November 16 at 4:24:57 a.m. ET.

OpenCode is an open source coding agent that lets consumers connect to more than 200 model providers or local models, including Anthropic’s Claude models, OpenAI’s GPTs, Google’s Gemini, DeepSeek, and Z.ai’s GLM. Jesta doesn’t know which model the attacker used, as there was nothing in the traffic that named the model. OpenCode's web fetch tool, however, did name itself, so Jesta knows the attacker used this coding agent - not a scanner - to do the dirty work.

It has been revealed that “Nothing in OpenCode was built for hacking,” Finkelshtein said in a Tuesday report about the agent-led attack. But, he added, nothing in the coding agent “stops you from pointing it at someone else's website either. When you do, the agent goes through the site the same way it goes through code. It reads, tries something, reads the result and tries the next thing, for as long as you let it run.”.

That’s what it did in this operation, which took less than six minutes and cost the human operator nothing.

Sources indicate that the first call came from a Chrome browser on a Mac, requesting the front page of one of the financial firm’s systems. The site refused it, and six seconds later, the same IPv6 address in Bucharest, on an ordinary DIGI Romania business line, tried again. It used the same Chrome version, but noted it was an Android Pixel 10 phone (it wasn’t) to see if the site would let a phone in (it didn’t).

After failing to gain access through the front page, the agent asked the system for its API definition, which was also refused. Five seconds later, it tried a different address - this one was a decoy set up by Jesta - and it answered the agent, providing the readable file defining how the API works.

It has been revealed that the agent read the document, and 13 seconds later followed a link it contained. At 4:26:01 a.m. ET, Jesta’s defenses marked the website visitor as an AI agent, opened a case, and from here on out, everything the agent accessed was contained inside a fake environment designed to trick intruders. This included a phony key, which the attacker then used to attempt to break into the organization’s systems.

Sources indicate that “It worked like a developer,” Finkelshtein stated about the coding agent. “It read the API docs and did what they said. It found a key and used it. It checked whether the lock was real, then made up a key of its own and tried that. None of the threat feeds the customer has knew the address, so a blocklist would never have stopped it. The bar for doing this is now installing an app. Think about how many people can do that.”.

In addition to OpenCode, the attacker used only Chrome 157, both in desktop and mobile modes, and curl/8.7.1, a command-line tool that has shipped with every Mac since macOS 15. The agent passed information between the three tools. It included the planted key in a command-line request and then tested three scenarios – using the decoy key, no key, and a fabricated key – to determine whether what it found in the API documentation was legit.

Sources indicate that it also tried multiple URLs using the browser. While it ultimately identified a valid endpoint, it attempted to read from one that accepts only data submissions, so its request was blocked again. Five minutes and 44 seconds after the first request, it gave up, and the logs haven’t detected any activity from this same intruder since then.

The security shop and its customer disclosed the activity to law enforcement and told us it’s “being handled.”.

While the attacker wasn’t able to steal anything in this attempt, security teams still need to take note, according to Finkelshtein.

“No blocklist would have helped” detect the malicious traffic, he explained. “Most security tools still decide by asking whether an address is known to be bad, and for this one the answer was no. If that key had been real, it would have been in.”.

In a recent development, instead of blocklists, Finkelshtein suggests paying attention to what the visitor does. In this case, several of its actions gave it away - including following a link that only existed inside an API doc, using a desktop browser and a fake phone, then curl, all from the same address within minutes, and trying multiple keys - including one with a made up name and then no key - within seconds.

“Open source lets anyone build software without a big team,” Finkelshtein wrote in the Tuesday blog. “AI is doing the same for hacking. The skill is in the model, the model is a setting, and the person giving the instructions doesn't need to know how any of it works.” ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reinforcement Learning environments give new capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

Sources indicate that an environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

It has been revealed that an RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that reveals up in the upcoming RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

According to recent reports, every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, consumers of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a new paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

Recent findings suggest that we think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it.".

Sources indicate that the frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

It has been revealed that the dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

Industry observers note that the RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

Framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:.

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

It has been revealed that A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

According to recent reports, harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

The viewer indicates the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

Recent findings suggest that the Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

Here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

OpenEnv's Harbor integration can run the same task directories with an agent such as OpenCode and return the verifier's reward alongside the agent's trace.

The command downloads the dataset's tasks/ directories, runs one task in Docker, and writes the result. The default connection uses a temporary Gradio tunnel so the sandboxed agent can reach OpenEnv's model proxy. Read the verifier result and the number of model calls:.

In a recent development, A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

Sources indicate that neMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

Sources indicate that the best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

Open your dataset card and add this to the YAML header:.

In a recent development, that is the whole integration. Keep rl-environment, then list every framework that can load your files. If your environment works with a framework we have not registered yet, open a PR to the list of supported libraries.

The docs have the full reference.

Sources indicate that we opened PRs to tag some of the environments people already train on. If you maintain one of these, merge the PR and your environment indicates up in the filter.

The first version generates one default snippet per framework. Per-config snippets are next, so a repo with several task sets can show the right command for each. After that we will look at structural detection for frameworks with strict layouts. It would also be really cool build custom task UIs, we’ve been experimenting with this here:.

Industry observers note that the bigger goal is for framework tagging to be automatic everywhere. OpenEnv already does it on upload. If you maintain Harbor, Verifiers, Nemo Gym, or any other environment framework, add the tags in your push path. It is a few lines, and every environment your owners publish becomes visible to everyone else.

If you train agents, go browse the filter. If you build environments, publish and tag them, whether they cover coding, tool use, games, robotics, or another task. Include the files, a working run command, and the rule that produces the reward so others can use them. If your framework is missing, contribute it to the list of supported libraries.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that easy-to-use, popular, not collecting data for us, or serving our ads? Down with you!

Arm is swinging the hammer at an enthusiast’s site hosting a bloat-free version of its instruction reference documentation, demanding it be taken offline after several years of availability.

The demand from Arm lawyers to Jon Palmisciano concern Jon’s Arm Reference, a site that provides the same arm Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) info available on Arm’s site, but with what Palmisciano describes as “without a million popups and all of the bloat” that Arm provides on its own.

According to recent reports, according to Palmisciano, his copy of the Arm ISA was culled from machine-readable XML files and stripped of the bloat. He built his version in 2022 with new CSS on top of it, and the addition of a quick search feature that, according to his comments on Hacker News, isn’t available in the official version.

“The aim has always been to make it the most comfortable and bullshit-free browsing experience for people who need these docs daily,” Palmisciano wrote in HN. Based on the responses the site seems to have plenty of fans.

Arm doesn’t care if Palmisciano’s project is well intentioned or for the benefit of the many software developers that write code for its chipsets, either: They want it offline by December 4 – 10 days from the publication of this story – or else.

As for what is going to happen, it seems like Jon’s Arm Reference will likely cease to exist in a little over a week – at least in its current form.

“Ideally I'd love to just get permission from Arm to keep the site up, but I'm pretty pessimistic about that,” Palmisciano told us. That noted, Palmisciano has “already seen a few archives and mirrors already.” The HN thread discussing the takedown order includes links to several versions, and Palmisciano has another trick up his sleeve that he’s considering playing: Open-sourcing the software he used to build his ISA page.

“I'd also consider open-sourcing my tooling so that people can (for their own private use) turn the original XML downloads from Arm into an identical site they can host locally,” Palmisciano told us. He said that he'll likely tweet about opening the tooling if he does do so. He's also considered directing the URL for Jon's Arm reference to point to the open-source tool, but Arm wants the subdomain it's hosted on removed from his site as well, so that may not happen.

Arm has been in touch to defend itself as well, saying that Arm appreciates the efforts of people like Palmisciano, but that it still has to protect its brand, and documentation.

In other words, if you’re an Arm dev worried about losing a valuable resource and having to turn to a website that bombards you with junk just to look up a few simple opcodes and operands you’d better find a backup host before next month.

That noted, Arm is willing to work something out with Palmisciano, the company told us.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Holo4 is our new series of agentic models.
  • Sources indicate that holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs.
  • Holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Holo4 is our new series of agentic models. It comes in two sizes: 27B dense and 35B-A3B Mixture of Experts. Both are available on the H Models API. We are also releasing an updated version of Holotron 3: Holotron4 Nano.

Sources indicate that holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs. It scores well on academic benchmarks, but we built it for real business workflows. It was trained through supervised and reinforcement learning on a large set of environments and tasks, including those generated by our Agentic Task Factory.

Holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools. It uses whichever fits the task. Most agentic models are trained for one interface only: GUI-focused models are blind without a screen, while models that prefer tool calling are stuck in front of an application that has no API. Real work is not siloed that way, and a single business task can require combining these different approaches.

According to recent reports, holo4 runs on desktops, on the web, on Android, in a code sandbox and against business APIs. It is the same model in each case and it is called the same way. You do not need to select a different model for each platform.

Holo4 models improve significantly over their Qwen base. Holo4 trails only the strongest closed models on long workflows: on OSWorld 2.0, Holo4 27B scores 61.7% against 81.8% for Opus 5.5, and Holo4 35B-A3B reaches 30.9%. However, it does so with orders of magnitude fewer parameters and at a much lower cost. We open-source every trajectory behind our scores on public benchmarks: replay each step at trajectories.hcompany.ai or download them from Hugging Face.

On the hardest academic benchmarks for desktop control (OSWorld 2.0) and API use (AutomationBench), Holo4 competes with frontier models at a much lower cost per task.

Sources indicate that OSWorld 2.0. Costs are estimated from the input and output tokens of each agentic run. Holo4 is priced at H Models API rates (single run). Qwen3.8 27B: model card score, cost from the tokens of our run at Alibaba Cloud list prices. Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: single run in our harness, at Alibaba Cloud list prices with cache hits at 20% of the input price. OpenAI launch data supplies the GPT and Opus effort sweeps; other closed and open-weight points use the official OSWorld 2.0 leaderboard. Releases, harnesses and task subsets differ. The line connects non-dominated score and cost pairs among the closed models; Holo4 is excluded.

AutomationBench. Holo4, Qwen3.8 27B and Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: AutomationBench v1.0.6, scores and costs measured in our internal harness. Other models: public-set scores from the AutomationBench README, cost per task from the official leaderboard, which runs on the private set. We will report Holo4 on the private set once it is evaluated.

Recent findings suggest that trained on environments and tasks from our Agentic Task Factory, Holo4 models excel on professional software. The examples below show Holo4 27B alongside Qwen3.8 27B, its base model. Same prompt and harness for both models.

Build a 3D model of the Eiffel Tower in FreeCAD, at a scale of 1 mm to 1 metre, centred on the origin and aligned to the X and Y axes. Work to this design.

The tower is square in blueprint at every height, never round. Its half-width, measured from the central axis out to the corner, is 62.5 mm at ground level, 32.5 mm at height 57, 17.5 mm at height 115, and 9.35 mm at height 276. Between those heights the half-width follows a smooth curve that falls steeply near the ground and gently higher up, never a straight line.

According to recent reports, four identical legs, one per quadrant, each a square column whose outer corner follows that profile. Each leg is 14 mm across at the ground and tapers to 4 mm at height 276. The legs stand apart from the ground up to the first platform, and converge as they rise. Nothing fills the space between them: the tower is open, and you can see straight through it from every side.

Three platforms, each a solid square slab centred on the axis: 72 mm across and 4 mm thick at height 57; 40 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 115; 22 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 276.

A mast from height 276 to 324, square, 8 mm across at its base tapering to 2 mm at the tip.

Every part must be a closed solid with non-zero volume, and no part may fill the space between the legs.

Holo4 27B (84 calls, 1.3M tokens).

Qwen3.8 27B (60 calls, 1.0M tokens).

Build a 3D model in FreeCAD of the H company logo: a solid filled disc beside a blocky sans-serif capital letter H, both extruded to the same thickness, the two shapes of similar height and set apart so they do not overlap, with the centre of the disc level with the middle of the H. Colour both shapes black.

Holo4 27B (94 calls, 1.5M tokens).

Qwen3.8 27B (118 calls, 1.9M tokens).

Build a Pac-Man-style game in Godot and leave it running.

It has been revealed that A rectangular maze of walls laid out on a grid, with pellets filling every open corridor. A player marker moves continuously along the corridors, eating each pellet it passes over and scoring a point for it. Three ghosts move through the same corridors and chase the player. If a ghost catches the player, the player loses a life and everything resets to its starting position. Score and lives are drawn on screen.

No one is going to play this. The player drives itself with a simple heuristic: at each junction it heads toward the nearest pellet, unless a ghost is close, in which case it moves away from the ghost. The game must run unattended and indefinitely, with no keyboard input at all.

When it works, start the game and leave it playing.

Holo4 27B (68 calls, 2.4M tokens, 268 lines).

Qwen3.8 27B (197 calls, 11.4M tokens, 327 lines).

According to recent reports, our internal set of agentic pipelines builds interactive environments and verifiable tasks from documentation alone, such as screenshots of real websites or open-source software. So far it has produced about 10,000 tasks across web apps, MCP servers and desktop environments, including hybrid environments that expose the same state through a GUI and MCP.

Recent findings suggest that alongside training, we rebuilt our harness, the loop that executes the model's actions and manages its context over hundreds of steps, using feedback from agentic performance on OSWorld 2.0. Agents tagged why each task failed and engineers reviewed their fixes. The largest changes were giving the agent a reliable memory that can keep track of hundreds of steps, and a shell on the desktop machine itself.

Opus 5 (70.2%) and GPT-5.6 Sol (66.2%) use max-effort partial rewards on the v2026.08.08 offline set from OpenAI's launch chart, as in the cost-performance plot. Other reference scores come from model cards and the official leaderboard. Task releases, subsets and harnesses vary.

Our post-training stack is designed to adapt to newly introduced foundation models and produce agents that generalize across interfaces and environments. As a member of the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition, we applied our latest stack to the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model as a follow-up to Holotron 3.

The same recipe turns Nemotron 3 Nano Omni into Holotron4 Nano, a generalist agentic model that significantly improves over the base model on GUI workflows and in environments exposing MCP, APIs or coding sandboxes.

Gains are absolute percentage-point improvements over Nemotron 3 Nano Omni.

These gains show that our recipe transfers well and can turn a generalist model into an agentic expert. Nothing in it is size-specific.

Sources indicate that both sizes are available today on the H Models API. Weights are on Hugging Face in BF16, FP8, NVFP4 and 4-bit GGUF, next to our small model, Holotron4 Nano.

We will release optimized DSpark drafter checkpoints in the coming days to further accelerate inference.

#116109. Tech Report: Bypassing iOS Safari 60 FPS Limit

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2167 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rida ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Bypassing iOS Safari 60 FPS Limit

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2167 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rida

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Devon Govett of React Aria posted “Scrolling is All You Need: Building a Swipeable Sheet” back in October, and in it he talked about his team developing a sheet component that cleverly leverages the physics and smooth interactions provided by native browsers to provide the illusion of a native interaction.
  • Industry observers note that more recently, Jordan Walke, creator of React, posted a video of an experiment on X showing a convincing native-like mobile interaction using DOM & CSS.
  • Sources indicate that what the video Jordan Walke posted doesn’t show is that, unless you flip the “Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps” flag buried deep within the Safari developer settings on iOS, WebKit limits requestAnimationFrame to just 60 Hz on a 120 Hz screen, and on a regular page, touch and pointer events are held to that same rate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rida F'kih · November 20, 2026 · 10 min read.

Devon Govett of React Aria posted “Scrolling is All You Need: Building a Swipeable Sheet” back in October, and in it he talked about his team developing a sheet component that cleverly leverages the physics and smooth interactions provided by native browsers to provide the illusion of a native interaction.

Industry observers note that more recently, Jordan Walke, creator of React, posted a video of an experiment on X showing a convincing native-like mobile interaction using DOM & CSS. It re-established a long-lived itch that I’ve had, and prompted this response from me. It’s something I could never justify building, however. Anything I built using this method would be pegged to 60 FPS.

Sources indicate that what the video Jordan Walke posted doesn’t show is that, unless you flip the “Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps” flag buried deep within the Safari developer settings on iOS, WebKit limits requestAnimationFrame to just 60 Hz on a 120 Hz screen, and on a regular page, touch and pointer events are held to that same rate. This is what makes even the best mobile websites feel irritating to use.

Industry observers note that how can I make this experience suck less without resorting to flags? Let’s call back to the React Aria piece. The reason it feels so nice is that scrolling is the responsibility of the compositor. It runs in its own thread. It moves, clips and fades without a JavaScript round-trip.

Finger to digitizer, digitizer to compositor, compositor to GPU. This will become the basis of our interaction.

Behold, two grids. They both move a square when you drag. The one on the left uses JavaScript events and sets the transform attribute in CSS, while the one on the right simply places a square in a scrollable area.

If you’re on iOS Safari, you’ll immediately be able to tell which is which because one refreshes at most 60 times a second in a renderer pass, while the other uses the compositor.

According to recent reports, in order to leverage the power of the scroll area, we need to find a way to read the scroll position outside of the renderer. If we can do that, we can treat it like a trackpad, or use it to “extract” native bounce, physics, momentum, etc., and apply them directly from the compositor to our animations.

The point is, it’d be crazy flexible if we could just find a way to pull the values out of it frequently enough.

Industry observers note that I measured scroll events updating 5 to 26 times per second during momentum scroll on an iPhone Duo. The best-case scenario is during slow, deliberate scrolls where it reaches almost 60 updates a second. Useless.

Instead, we’ll be aiming to read scrollTop and scrollLeft synchronously.

First, I tried having a MessageChannel call itself recursively, which worked: but it produced 50,000 reads a second with just 80 distinct values. That’s a lot of waste and heat since it pins a CPU core.

It has been revealed that next failure was trying to use Atomics to wake at the screen’s refresh rate, which worked and similarly extracted 80 distinct positions every second, but the drawbacks were too great. Since it needs a SharedArrayBuffer, we’re forced to use COOP/COEP headers which break cross-origin assets on our website.

What finally worked was using a MessageChannel like before, throttling the next measurement to the next tick using a setTimeout according to the refresh rate of the device, phase-locked to vsync using requestAnimationFrame timestamps. I was nervous about this approach, but as you’ll see later, it panned out well. The only remaining drawback specific to this solution was easy to work around. iOS rounds performance.now() to the millisecond, so I derived the minimum time between draws from the refresh interval.

According to recent reports, each solution got us 80 position reads per second. Two-thirds towards our goal of 120 Hz input.

Safari’s UI process sends the web process one scroll position at a time, and waits for an acknowledgement from the web process before sending another. Anything that arrives in the meantime is overwritten. This was costing us dropped positions. Digging through WebKit yielded what we needed to get around this. It turns out that on every tick where the page has a rendering upgrade queued, Safari flushes the position without waiting. An empty requestAnimationFrame loop is all we need to do that.

This bought us ~12.5% more reads, and brought us to 90 unique position reads per second.

I sort of assumed I had hit the limit of the aforementioned IPC, but it turns out that ProMotion was just deciding that there’s no need to render at a refresh rate higher than 90 Hz.

In a recent development, squeezing out the last 30 Hz was trickier. A GPU-accelerated CSS animation lets the screen go to 120 Hz, but only while something is scrolling. So a tiny invisible scroller smooth-scrolls in the background, ready to boost us to the full ProMotion refresh rate whenever we need it.

Of course, we don’t want the display pegging to 120 Hz the entire time, so we reserve all the tricks we used to get there for times we expect animations to occur: touch events, scroll-derived animations, etc.

If the interaction you’re building doesn’t need momentum, rubber banding, or snapping, you can forego them entirely and just use a passive touchmove listener on the controller which fires at the full 120 Hz.

Just like that, we’re receiving updates from the controller at a full 120 Hz! Drag the grid below to see.

One problem remains. scrollTop and scrollLeft are rounded to the nearest integer even though iOS scrolls with sub-point precision. Easy fix, thankfully. We just scale the scrollable surface up by the device pixel ratio, then its container back down by its reciprocal.

If you want to use the viewport itself as a controller, you can choose to invasively set the initial-scale in the same way, but this comes with some caveats. You’ll have to scale units by the DPR, disable text autosizing, and manually scale safe areas. You’ll also get tiny text-selection indicators. All trade-offs, but by no means required.

From here on out, I’ll refer to these scrolling grids as “controllers”, because they act exactly like one. All we have to do is make one invisible and lay it over where we want to read high-frequency input.

Note that the page itself can also be a controller, but Safari will throttle reported scroll positions to 10 Hz during the URL bar resize that happens when you change scroll direction. WebKit skips this if we give the page a scroll-driven animation that animates a non-GPU-accelerated attribute. I went with transitioning between two transparent colours for this page.

Now we get high-frequency input, but the DOM still only updates 60 times a second, so if we tried to leverage it as it stands, we’d just be updating a value twice for every frame that’s drawn. The user would get no benefit.

It has been revealed that the vast majority of dragging interactions are already covered by our controllers, and predefined animations are covered by CSS animations. But what about more complicated interactions? What about computation-derived layouts? What about shaders?

Industry observers note that ask your search engine or AI of choice today “How to render canvas content on iOS at 120 Hz without feature flag?” and it will respond that this is a fundamental impossibility in iOS Safari. Even WebKit’s own bug tracker is full of people asking for it. Ink & Switch, game-engine makers. People even cite Capacitor & Tauri as resorting to private APIs.

Asking Google yields the following preamble.

There is no public web API or standard JavaScript workaround to force HTML5 (requestAnimationFrame) to run at 120 Hz on iOS Safari without changing the system feature flag.

Fable 5.2 shares the same sentiment.

Short answer: you can't, for JavaScript-drawn canvas frames. On iOS, WebKit caps page rendering updates (which is when canvas content is presented) at 60 Hz unless the user turns off the flag. No web API overrides it. […] Timer-based loops (setTimeout, MessageChannel) won't help, in my understanding: you can draw more often, but the result is still presented at the 60 Hz rendering enhancement. Low Power Mode throttles further.

In a recent development, at first, I tunnel-visioned on scroll. I tried breaking workers, pre-rendering permutation “flip-books,” and even live-generating video. It was all too laggy, jagged, or required so much RAM the WebKit process just crashed.

Seven attempts later, and a whole lot of agents digging through WebKit’s source, I landed on this.

Sources indicate that in WebKit on iOS, if we create a canvas element and call transferControlToOffscreen, we get an OffscreenCanvas back. The original canvas element becomes a placeholder, and WebKit (following the HTML specification’s recommendation) skips waiting for the next rendering pass when an OffscreenCanvas pushes a frame.

Unlike earlier attempts, without workarounds this is easy on the battery and only uses as much memory as is needed to support a higher-frequency backing store.

Jackpot. We now have 120 FPS rendering on iOS WebKit canvases.

Recent findings suggest that now we can take any input at 120 Hz, and render an output at that very same frame rate. The first thing I created for this was a small UI clone of Ando’s mobile application fitted with a Liquid Glass tab bar, buttons, and buttery smooth navigation interactions. Once installed as a PWA, I kept having to double-take to check I wasn’t in the native application.

In a recent development, this page is fitted with two custom “Liquid Glass” elements in the viewport. Each of them renders at the full device refresh rate. We have to be very deliberate in order to do this in a way that is performant and convincing.

Recent findings suggest that when the page first loads, we take a snapshot and load it into a WebGL texture. This texture is used as the foundation for a composite that is then fed into our shader.

As the page scrolls, we then sample the region beneath each component, which is all we need to produce our effect. Building it this way means that no matter how the content below it is built, it can decide the best way to keep the texture live.

On this page, components using requestAnimationFrame for illustrative reasons update the texture from the main thread. Components using OffscreenCanvas post their frames directly from their workers to the worker managing the texture. This keeps us off the main thread and lets us get shaders refreshing at 120 Hz.

After all that, the glass just samples a small region around where it would land on the composite texture and computes the frame.

According to recent reports, let’s build our Liquid Glass tab bar. We’ll start out by just drawing the underlying structure.

Recent findings suggest that we’ll break this down into one controller for each button. Each controller sends us timestamped events: which controller is being used, and how much it has been dragged. We keep a short history of those samples, so we know when a press has moved far enough to count as a drag, and how fast the finger is moving. Nothing else. Everything else is derived from that.

We now build a state machine around this. Every frame, the newly introduced events go in, and a frame comes out: where the lens is, how far it has lifted and stretched, and how visible the pill is.

Finally, we apply some shaders to get a convincing Liquid Glass effect.

I built a benchmark environment and recorded an iPhone 18 Pro at 240 FPS, slowing it down to an eighth to benchmark the difference. The two oscillating squares measure inputs and renders.

Over three seconds of dragging, the controller version averaged 118 FPS while the pointer events version held a steady 60. Even in Low Power Mode, which traditionally limits you to 30, this approach gets you 60.

Liquid Glass was the target as an overblown example, but this unlocks a lot. For the first time, you can take input and render output at true device-native speeds on iOS Safari. Micro-interactions feel native and delightful, PWAs which ignored the aforementioned feature flag finally have a way to render at 120 Hz, and look at all the fun we had along the way!

Would I rebuild my entire application around this? No. Fact remains it’s completely within Apple’s rights and would not violate the HTML specification if they just decided to make OffscreenCanvas’ placeholder wait for the main thread rendering pass. They even have a strong track record of “party pooping” as was done shortly after Lochie Axon unveiled the web-haptics library. I’d much prefer they make these findings moot by disabling the feature flag and natively supporting ProMotion for websites, but Apple is Apple for a reason after all.

JEP 545 Moves ZGC Memory Preparation off the Startup Path in JDK 28

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (948 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News JEP 545 Moves ZGC Memory Preparation off the Startup Path in JDK 28.
  • Nov 23, 2026 4 min read.
  • JEP 545, Faster Startup and Warmup with ZGC, has been integrated into JDK 28, moving the work of acquiring and preparing heap memory off the startup path and onto dedicated concurrent worker threads.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News JEP 545 Moves ZGC Memory Preparation off the Startup Path in JDK 28.

Nov 23, 2026 4 min read.

JEP 545, Faster Startup and Warmup with ZGC, has been integrated into JDK 28, moving the work of acquiring and preparing heap memory off the startup path and onto dedicated concurrent worker threads. On Linux 6.1 and later it also upgrades 4 KB pages to 2 MB pages while the application runs. The 2 MB initial heap behind the JEP's headline numbers comes from elsewhere: adaptive heap sizing, in the companion JEP 546, which still defaults to off.

In a recent development, deploying ZGC has until now meant choosing which half of a trade-off to pay for. The collector's pause times do not grow with the heap, but its collection frequency does, so a small heap brings on early and frequent cycles. The JEP describes the older ergonomic behavior of committing one sixty-fourth of physical memory for the initial heap.

According to recent reports, A team chasing fast startup set a tiny -Xms and accepted a long warmup, because the collector then had to acquire and prepare memory in increments while the application was already allocating. A team chasing fast warmup set a large -Xms, usually with -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch, and paid the whole bill before the first request landed. The JEP puts the spread at roughly a tenth of a second to start with a 2 MB heap against more than ten seconds with a 32 GB one on current hardware.

That work now happens in a newly introduced thread, ZMemoryWorker, one per heap partition. It commits and uncommits memory concurrently as capacity changes. It also heats memory before application threads reach it, which means pre-touching page by page and collapsing small pages into large ones.

Industry observers note that the budget is fixed rather than adaptive. ZConcurrentWorkersCPUShare in zGlobals.hpp is 0.25, so preparation takes at most a quarter of the available CPU. ZGC's director caps young-generation worker counts when adaptive sizing is on, which keeps collection inside its CPU target while expansion continues and the collector deliberately runs above its heuristic heap size target.

Industry observers note that large pages on Linux no longer require an administrator to reserve them up front. ZGC probes for MADV_COLLAPSE, the madvise mode added in Linux 6.1, by mapping a 4 MB region, pre-touching a single page and collapsing an aligned 2 MB range. When the probe succeeds and memory heating is enabled, the collector enters a fresh Collapse state and upgrades pages in the background. The call races the kernel's khugepaged, so the implementation retries on EAGAIN.

The change indicates up in what a deployer no longer has to decide. Where JDK 25 forced a choice between two tunings, JDK 28 offers a third option:.

It has been revealed that the third command produces the JEP's case study figures, a 38% drop in startup time and a fall in warmup from 80 seconds to 10 for Spring PetClinic on a 32 GB machine. -XX:+ZAdaptiveHeapSizing takes the minimum and initial heap down to 2 MB and raises the MaxHeapSize ceiling to 100% of physical memory. Without it, ZGC falls back to the shared heap sizing path and a 25% ceiling. Concurrent preparation still runs, but not the aggressive expansion the measurements depend on.

It has been revealed that using identical memory techniques on every operating system is an explicit non-goal, so large pages may be the default on Linux and not on Windows. The JEP also cautions that applications tuned around a larger initial heap may warm up more slowly and need re-tuning.

Sources indicate that two further edges live in the implementation rather than the text. Pairing -XX:+UseLargePages with adaptive sizing and no -Xmx logs a warning and disables explicit large pages for the heap. The retry loop around MADV_COLLAPSE can also spin indefinitely when EAGAIN persists, a case the code attributes to pinning through mlock or long-term DMA and treats as user error.

Teams can see the heap sizing difference for themselves on the JDK 28 early-access builds by comparing the resolved flags:.

The second run drops the minimum and initial sizes to the 2 MB floor and lifts the maximum from a quarter of physical memory to all of it. Adding -Xlog:gc+init reports Memory Heating: Enabled and, once the collapse path is active, Large Page Support: Enabled (Transparent, JVM enforced).

Services already running a modest heap on Linux 6.1 or later pick up concurrent pre-touch and background large pages without touching a flag, because memory heating is on by default. Services carrying a large pre-touched heap purely to buy warmup have something to delete, though only after enabling adaptive sizing. That 100% ceiling reads worse than it behaves. The policy tracks machine-wide memory and holds a reserve, preferring to leave a fifth of the machine free, fighting for a tenth and enforcing a twentieth, with those margins widening when usage is unstable or compressed.

It has been revealed that JDK 28 reaches Rampdown Phase One on December 3, 2026, with general availability scheduled for March 9, 2027. The JEP's own future work points at better CPU sharing between concurrent collection and concurrent commit, and at ahead-of-time compilation from JEP 544, already Completed for JDK 28, which frees JIT cycles the memory workers could spend instead.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Inception, a new data theft and extortion gang that security researchers have theorized is a rebrand of the ShinyHunters group, “reject[s] this attribution” and claims it has no affiliation with any prior cybercrime enterprise.

In a lengthy statement posted Tuesday and shared on X, the extortionists insist that they are a new group, with new operators, and that their alleged social engineering attacks aren’t copying anyone - but rather just abusing the weakest link in an organization’s security: “a human being holding a phone.”.

The rant follows a Monday report by Okta Threat Intelligence - along with social media speculation since Inception’s inception last week - that the newly emerged group is very likely ShinyHunters with a different name.

Okta’s researchers based their analysis on the two groups’ shared infrastructure, plus Inception’s nearly identical tactics: voice phishing, during which the scammers trick targets into entering credentials into phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA) requests.

According to recent reports, inception apparently took offense to this. “We would like to address this once, clearly, and only once,” the crims' statement states. “We are not ShinyHunters. We were never ShinyHunters. We are Inception.”.

According to recent reports, the gang argues that its overlapping domain registrars, hosting providers, and DNS services don’t prove anything. These are commodity services, “available to anyone who can pay for them,” Inception wrote.

Plus, their similar methodologies don't necessarily make Inception a reboot. “That is not theft of tradecraft,” they wrote. “It is acknowledgment of a good idea – the same way every group after LockBit used a leak site, and nobody called them LockBit.”.

“Inception is a new group, with new operators, our own objectives, and our own name,” the statement continues. “What we share with the past is plumbing.”.

To be fair, the new crime crew has every reason to distance itself from ShinyHunters.

That gang’s September FBI hack - plus several earlier digital heists during which the criminals stole information belonging to millions of people, including cancer patients, university and K-12 students - put a massive target on its collective backs.

And while at least three ShinyHunters suspects were arrested in September and October, there's no confirmation that authorities have dismantled the entire operation.

Plus, as a ShinyHunters spokesperson told The Register in an earlier interview, they and others in the crew started off as GnosticPlayers before rebranding as ShinyHunters in 2020 - so a reboot isn’t beyond the realm of possibility.

According to recent reports, inception, for its part, states it “will not comment further on the ghost of ShinyHunters,” and it has its own work to do. And by work, it means copying ShinyHunters' playbook, stealing corporate data, and extorting victim companies for massive sums of money.®.

#116106. Tech Report: Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

📖 Baca

Tech Report: Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

📅 29 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1828 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage.
  • Sources indicate that our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap.
  • Recent findings suggest that consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this plan includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an agent can call a search tool, inspect a structured patient or account record, query a database, and pull metadata, then weave all of it into one answer. That m aakes the usual question of factuality more subtle than it looks. Most of the systems built to check LLM answers, from RAGAS faithfulness to fine-grained checkers like MiniCheck, AlignScore, and SummaC, ask whether a claim is supported by the available evidence once that evidence has been pooled together. In their usual form, they do not tell us which MCP tool output supports each claim, or whether that is the source the answer names.

Sources indicate that our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap. The failure mode we care about is one we call cross-source conflation: a claim that is true somewhere in the evidence, but attributed to the wrong source. A source-blind verifier may pass it, because the fact does exist in the pool. A source-aware verifier should not.

Recent findings suggest that consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this plan includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to. Pool the two together and the claim looks supported. Keep them separate and the attribution is wrong, and in a data-sensitive setting a wrong attribution can be as damaging as a wrong fact. The same pattern reveals up in a clinical agent, where a patient-specific medication detail taken from a patient-history tool becomes misleading the moment the answer presents it as a finding from the medical literature.

It has been revealed that A claim can be supported by one MCP source while the answer attributes it to another. Source-blind scoring sees support in the pooled evidence and passes it; ProvenanceGuard separately checks whether the supporting source matches the one the answer states or implies. Source: paper Figure 1.

This is why faithfulness scores, useful as they are, are not enough for MCP agents. An answer carries provenance, sometimes explicitly ("according to the account record") and sometimes implicitly. ProvenanceGuard keeps that connection between claim and source available for inspection.

Industry observers note that provenanceGuard is a post-generation verification layer that sits on top of a black-box MCP agent. It runs after an agent produces an answer, and never collapses the evidence into one anonymous context. Instead it carries the source identity all the way through the pipeline. It reads the captured MCP trace, including the tool outputs and their source IDs, without retraining the agent. Then it does five things in sequence: it breaks the answer into specific claims, finds the source most relevant to each one, checks whether that source actually supports it, compares the source with the one the answer names or implies, and finally emits both a per-claim source verdict and a global, answer-level allow or block decision.

In a recent development, the verification flow. Source identity is preserved through decomposition, routing, support scoring, attribution checking, and repair, rather than being pooled. Blocked answers can go through RARR-style repair and be re-verified. Source: paper Figure 2.

Recent findings suggest that A few of the design choices are worth calling out. For the experiments in our paper, we used local models so the captured traces could be processed in a controlled, offline setup: MiniLM helps find the relevant source, a DeBERTa NLI verifier model checks whether that source supports the claim, and a local language model helps break answers into claims. The verifier also checks literal values closely: a number, date, or identifier absent from the source cannot pass merely because the sentence sounds plausible. A calibrated decision step combines these signals. If an answer is blocked, a RARR-style repair step can try a source-grounded revision or a safe fallback, which the verifier then checks again.

Recent findings suggest that those named models are the setup we evaluated, not a requirement of ProvenanceGuard. The same claim, source, and decision steps can be adapted to hosted models where a team prefers cloud services; a upcoming setup would need its own testing and calibration. Our reported results come from the local configuration. Its conservative decision policy suits data-sensitive review, where getting the source right matters more than producing the fastest possible answer.

According to recent reports, we tested ProvenanceGuard on answers from a medical agent that had used patient records, research articles, and other tools. This gave us 281 real traces to study. Medicine is a useful test because a fact from a patient's record and a fact from general research cannot be treated as the same source. The method can also be used in other fields when an agent keeps a record of its tool outputs and source IDs. For the main test, human experts checked 361 claims from 40 answers set aside from the data used to develop the system.

The most direct result is this: experts said 139 claims should not pass, and ProvenanceGuard caught 138 of them. It let one through. It also held 67 claims that the experts considered supported, sending them for review or repair. This reflects the cautious setting we tested: it favors a second look at some supported claims over letting unsupported ones through. For claims with an identifiable source, it also picked the right source about 86% of the time in this test.

Sources indicate that we ran four other support checkers on the same claims. ProvenanceGuard scored highest on the paper's measure of how well a system catches claims that should be blocked while avoiding unnecessary blocks. The other checkers in this comparison did not tell us which tool output supported each claim. ProvenanceGuard records that connection, so a reviewer can see the source checked for each claim and the decision it produced.

Binary support metrics on the same held-out claim packet. ProvenanceGuard matches or beats the source-blind baselines on blocking while also producing per-claim source verdicts. Source: paper abstract and Table III.

It has been revealed that in a separate, harder test with several similar sources, ProvenanceGuard scored 0.846 F1 for deciding which claims to block, but identified the exact source correctly in 50.3% of claims. Telling similar sources apart remains an vital area for improvement.

We also ran a controlled test focused on wrong attribution: we changed the named source in 50 cases while leaving the supporting evidence intact. ProvenanceGuard caught all 50 swaps. This reveals it can detect a clear source error, while the harder test shows the challenge of choosing among many plausible sources.

Blocking is only useful if there is something to do with a blocked answer. Wired to the RARR-style repair loop, the full-trace run resolved all 173 blocked answers, though 144 of them ended in fallback text rather than a substantive rewrite, which is the system choosing to avoid an unverifiable answer rather than manufacture one. On reconstructed multi-source test traces, a fresh repair run resolved all 59 initially blocked answers with only two terminal fallbacks. As an offline gate the overhead is modest, roughly half a second per answer on the reported local configuration, with the NLI and routing calls themselves in the tens of milliseconds.

As agents move from single-passage RAG to multi-tool MCP setups, the question of which source a fact actually came from stops being a footnote and becomes part of what factuality means. ProvenanceGuard makes that source connection visible claim by claim. For Multiverse Computing, that means a way to check existing agents while keeping sensitive traces in a controlled environment when needed. The medical study is one use case; the same approach can be adapted wherever an agent's trace preserves its tools and sources.

That adaptation is already visible in NVIDIA NVFlow, which merged an optional grounding-verification stage for its finance agent. It checks completed answers against the SEC excerpts the agent retrieved and saves separate decisions without changing the original rollout or training data. The NVFlow contribution uses ProvenanceGuard's source-aware verification approach; the repair loop discussed above belongs to the broader research system.

ProvenanceGuard was also presented as a poster at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 at UC Berkeley.

Want the full technical details, including the routing and NLI derivations, the calibration ablations, the multi-source stress slices, and the complete results tables? Read the full paper on Hugging Face, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying source-aware verification to your own agents.

The failure mode that matters for MCP agents is quieter than "hallucination": a claim that is true somewhere in the pooled tool outputs, attributed to the wrong source.

Source-blind faithfulness can still go green in that case — the fact exists in the soup. Source-aware verification is the contract upgrade: keep tool/source IDs through claim decomposition, support check, and attribution check, then allow/block with a per-claim source verdict a reviewer can actually inspect.

Practical ask for teams wiring MCP: when your eval indicates "grounded," does it mean supported-by-any-tool-output, or supported-by-the-source-the-answer-named? Those are different release gates. In multi-tool setups the second one is the one that catches cross-source conflation before a human trusts the citation.

Hi, thank you for your comment. You’ve captured the issue well. For ProvenanceGuard, when a claim is “grounded” it means it is supported by the source the answer names or implies. Finding the fact somewhere else in the tool outputs isn’t enough. In the refund-window example, the policy supports the fact, but the answer credits the account record, so we flag the mismatch and show the source verdict.

Industry observers note that I had a brief read on the paper, but I could not find any comparison with cheaper llm agent for source aware judge. Like this is my reading of the paper;.

Like, it seems (2 - 5) can be done via basic prompts in lifecycle, if you own the executing agent. If not, this can also be done via hooks in harness as plugin. Do you have any comparison on this. Basically, how much of random forest, and all of these eng/plumbing is buying, vs second llm call over traces+ans?

Industry observers note that hi, fair question. A source-aware LLM judge could do these checks, and we don’t report a direct comparison with a cheaper one in the paper.

However, part of our motivation is that introducing an LLM judge can itself give inconsistent verdicts or confuse sources (the same kinds of errors we’re trying to catch). A second LLM call can therefore introduce fresh errors of its own. ProvenanceGuard uses explicit source tracking and calibrated support checks to reduce reliance on another generative judgment. The comparison you suggest would indeed be a useful further study to quantify the benefit in accuracy, latency and cost.

The BPF verifier has historically worked by tracing every possible path of execution through a program, checking, at each instruction, that various safety properties hold. This works, but it can result in an exponential increase in the number of states that need checking in programs with complicated control-flow. Alexei Starovoitov, one of the kernel's core BPF maintainers, has shared a patch set that substantially reworks how the verifier tracks states, in order to reduce the size of that exponential explosion.

AI godfather Yann LeCun torches Anthropic CEO over AI gatekeeping

💡 Key Takeaways
  • ‘It’s like the Ottoman Empire banning the printing press for Arabic so they would keep in control of the dogma,’ he says.
  • Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is taking heat from AI luminary Yann LeCun, one of the founding fathers of modern machine learning, because of the Claudefather's fear-mongering around open-weights models, which also happen to compete with his products.
  • In an X post this week, LeCun likened the Amodei's advocacy to a “new form of medieval obscurantism.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

‘It’s like the Ottoman Empire banning the printing press for Arabic so they would keep in control of the dogma,’ he says.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is taking heat from AI luminary Yann LeCun, one of the founding fathers of modern machine learning, because of the Claudefather's fear-mongering around open-weights models, which also happen to compete with his products.

In an X post this week, LeCun likened the Amodei's advocacy to a “new form of medieval obscurantism.”.

“Dario’s spiel since GPT-2 has always been about hyping the dangers so that open models would be made illegal, and he would stay in control,” LeCun wrote in response to a now three-year-old video posted to the platform in which Amodei warned US Congress members about the dangers of open-weights models, the use of which could not be monitored or policed.

Sources indicate that “He left OpenAI because he wasn’t going to have control. It’s like the Ottoman Empire banning the printing press for Arabic so they would keep in control of the dogma.”.

LeCun is one of the most influential names in AI and ML. His team is credited with the development of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in the late ’80s during his time at Bell Labs. He later oversaw the development of Meta’s Llama herd of models as chief AI scientist before shifting gears away from LLMs to world model architectures like JEPA. He has also been a strong proponent of open source AI development and open models.

Of the major model houses, Anthropic has taken the most hostile position against the adoption of open-weights models.

Despite advocating against the unregulated diffusion of open models for years, Anthropic’s fearmonger-in-chief has maintained that the manufacturer isn’t opposed to them. “Anthropic has never advocated for a ban on open-weights models,” Amodei wrote in a blog post earlier this year.

The executive has instead fomented fears over their potential misuse.

“Open-weights models — it does not matter whether they come from China or anywhere else — do potentially present a higher risk than closed models, because it is very difficult to apply guardrails to them or monitor their usage, and, once weights are released, they cannot be withdrawn,” the blog post read.

Amodei has repeatedly hammered these talking points over the past several years, including in the Senate hearing that solicited LeCun’s post.

Amodei has also called for measures, such as stricter export controls on the export of high-end accelerators to China; a crackdown on industrial-scale distillation operations, for which his tech giant has previously accused Alibaba and other Chinese model devs; and mandating safety testing for sufficiently advanced open-weights models.

In other words, Anthropic doesn’t want all freely downloadable models banned, just the ones that Amodei thinks aren’t playing fair or are powerful enough to compete with its own.

LeCun isn’t the only one who has pushed back against anti-open-weights rhetoric in recent memory.

Earlier this summer, a cadre of tech titans, including Meta, Microsoft, IBM, Dell, and Nvidia, wrote an open letter [PDF] in support of open-weights models.

According to recent reports, open models “strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said at the time. “The world needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models.”.

As we previously reported, Nvidia’s future depends on its ability to sell to a diverse set of customers ranging from the big model houses like Anthropic and OpenAI to public clouds, neoclouds, and enterprises. And while many of these companies are perfectly happy to get their AI through Claude or ChatGPT, others, whether it be for regulatory or cost reasons, are not.

Earlier this month, we reported how British neobank Revolut cut their vibe coding tab by 10x by moving its roughly 2,000 employees from Claude to Z.AI’s GLM 5.1 running on a cluster of 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs.

The problem for Anthropic, and OpenAI for that matter, is the more enterprises that embrace open-weights models, the less likely they are to spring for Claude or ChatGPT.

The Register reached out to Anthropic for comment, but had not heard back at the time of publication. ®.

I assume you know about the P vs. NP problem. But what is this wacky thing Anthropic just posted?

You learned how to take a determinant in your linear algebra class:.

The naive way is fine for 3Ã3 matrices, but notice that you need to perform Î(n!) arithmetic operations here. Exercise for the reader is to find the exact number of operations (hint: start with a recurrence relation).

Luckily, if you paid attention, you will remember there are faster ways to do this for big nÃn matrices, like Gaussian elimination. If we stick only to adding and multiplying, we can still find a determinant in polynomial time (there are better ways, but this is an old, readable method).

According to recent reports, A related problem to the determinant is finding the permanent. Itâs like a determinant without any subtraction:.

According to recent reports, unlike determinants, there is no known way to compute permanents in polynomial time. Since finding the permanent of a matrix of 0s and 1s is NP-hard (and in fact #P-complete), it would be pretty important if there were a way.

What the Anthropic proof that VPâ VNP means is that there is no way to do this if we are limited to arithmetic circuits of size polynomial in the input-size, which look like this:.

According to recent reports, this means that for P to equal NP, there must be some trick to computing permanents using AND/OR/NOT on the bits of the input that is better than addition and multiplication. There are many problems where access to Boolean operators is helpful, but it isnât clear how they would help with the permanent. If you think of a way, go claim your $1 million.
