Breaking: Open TTS Leaderboard: Scalable Evaluation for Multilingual Text-to-Speech and Voice Cloning

📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1381 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible.
  • In a recent development, evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized.
  • These arenas compare models by presenting users with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible. On the Hugging Face Hub (as of Sep 30, 2026) there are more than 8K TTS models available 🚀.

In a recent development, evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized. The gold standard is human preference scores such as MOS or MUSHRA (more on metrics). To this end, several arena-based leaderboards have established themselves as useful reference points for the community:.

These arenas compare models by presenting users with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other. After collecting a sufficient number of votes, an Elo score is computed to rank models, typically with the Bradley–Terry model (see Voice Arena methodology).

While human preference is the ultimate decider, arenas cannot scale to keep up with the pace of TTS releases. This may partly explain why open-source models are underrepresented on arena-style leaderboards: as of Sep 30, 2026, only 16 of the 92 models on Artificial Analysis are open-weights, with a similar skew on Voice Arena. This likely reflects practical factors: adding an API model requires little more than an API key, whereas an open model must be hosted and served by the arena operator, and commercial providers have more reason to seek placement than open-source authors. Another limitation with arena-style evaluation is voter consistency: no arena can ensure that the same voters with the same criteria of “better” can consistently evaluate models over time. Even the preferences of a single person change over time (“A man cannot step into the same river twice” as famously remarked by Heraclitus).

To this end, we've built the Open TTS Leaderboard, which uses objective metrics to evaluate models on complementary aspects of performance:.

By relying on objective metrics evaluating a model drops from a couple weeks (for collecting votes) to a couple hours ⚡.

Importantly, the Open TTS Leaderboard does not replace human preference ranking. ASR-based WER provides a proxy for intelligibility, while speaker similarity estimates voice identity preservation. Neither directly measures naturalness, expressiveness, or listener preference. Nevertheless, they can even inform voting-based leaderboards which models to include in their evaluations.

Our intention with this leaderboard is for it to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. The next few sections give an overview of main features of the Open TTS Leaderboard.

From the default view of the leaderboard, models are ranked by macro-average WER on the English splits of Seed TTS Eval (paper) and CV3 Eval (zero shot) (paper).

hexgrad/Kokoro-82M, Supertone/supertonic-3, and fishaudio/s2-pro lead the pack on English WER when averaged on these two splits, while the Pareto plots visualize which models strike a good balance between WER, batched inference (RTFx), and size.

English performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

k2-fsa/OmniVoice, fishaudio/s2-pro, and FunAudioLLM/Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B-2512 are strong multilingual models.

By toggling “Voice cloning”, the models that support this functionality (on the selected languages) can be compared.

Moreover, a SIM column for speaker similarity now appears in the table, as well as two more Pareto plots for visualizing the tradeoff between SIM, batched inference, and size.

The average WER of some models, such as bosonai/higgs-tts-3-4b and openbmb/VoxCPM2, improve under voice cloning, namely when a reference audio is provided.

It has been revealed that numbers only tell part of the story, and as mentioned earlier human preference is the ultimate decider. From the “Listen” tab, you can compare the generated outputs that are behind the metrics, to find which model(s) you prefer!

Pick the language/dataset you're interested in, whether you want to compare voice cloning, and optionally pick the models or listen to outputs from a random selection.

The “Listen” tab fills an crucial gap in existing TTS leaderboards: a space to explore model outputs of various models.

Industry observers note that you can even give feedback on the generated outputs. As we collect more votes from the community, we may include this data on the leaderboard. So vote! But please login with your HF account to help us weed out spam/bots.

The “Streaming” tab compares the streaming capabilities. Models are ranked by TTFA (time-to-first-audio), which quantifies how long a user waits after probing a model in order to obtain audio that can be played. This is important for voice agents and other interactive apps.

For streaming models (✅ under “Streaming API”) it's the time until the first audio chunk arrives. For non-streaming models, it's the time until the whole utterance is generated, because playback can't start any earlier. Every model runs one audio at a time (batch size 1), on the same 50 English prompts from CV3-Eval, on the same hardware and in its default voice. We drop the first 3 runs as warm-up and report the median TTFA across the rest.

The default view compares performance on an H200 GPU. Results are also available for CPU for a small (but growing) set of models!

kyutai/pocket-tts is a great model for streaming on both GPU and CPU!

In a recent development, the goal of the Open TTS Leaderboard is not only to keep up with the incredible pace of TTS model releases, but to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. Let us know which datasets, models, and metrics you want to see!

In a recent development, we will soon open-source the evaluation scripts, much like the Open ASR Leaderboard repo, so that you can directly provide your feedback and suggestions via GitHub Issues and PRs! Let's shape TTS evaluations together 🤗.

Glad this board splits multilingual TTS quality from voice-cloning identity instead of one aggregate green.

The check I'd keep reading: whether the ranking still holds when you hold language/domain fixed versus when cloning is the axis. Otherwise teams optimize the easier subscale and still call the result "SOTA TTS.".

English performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has movie box audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

It has been revealed that open TTS Leaderboard is an open evaluation platform designed to make multilingual text-to-speech and voice-cloning models easier to compare at scale. Traditional TTS arenas usually let customers listen to outputs from two models and choose the one they prefer. Those votes can then be used to calculate an Elo-style score, often through approaches such as the Bradley–Terry model, giving users a simple way to understand how different systems perform based on human preference.

Recent findings suggest that human feedback remains an notable part of evaluating speech quality, but relying only on arena-style voting can be difficult as new TTS models are released at a rapid pace. Open-source models can also face practical barriers because they generally need to be hosted and served by the evaluation platform, while API-based commercial models can be added more easily. This can result in open-weight systems being less visible on public leaderboards. Another challenge is consistency: people's preferences and listening criteria can change over time, meaning that votes collected months apart may not always represent exactly the same standards.

Open TTS Leaderboard aims to address these challenges by providing a scalable and transparent space for evaluating multilingual TTS and voice-cloning systems. The goal is to make comparisons easier to reproduce, expand coverage of open models, and provide useful evaluation signals alongside human preference. By bringing together scalable testing and community feedback, the project can help researchers, developers, and people better understand how speech models perform across different languages, voices, and use cases.

GitHub repo with the eval scripts is public! https://github.com/huggingface/open-tts-leaderboard.

AutoSynthData: Generating Training Data for Enterprise Agents

📅 02 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2047 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments.
  • In a recent development, the difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data.
  • It has been revealed that at ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments. The work they ask these agents to do is shaped by the systems they use, the rules they follow, and the state of their data. A model may be broadly capable and still struggle with a particular environment: a workflow it handles poorly, a combination of tools it misuses, or a constraint it fails to respect. Those are the weaknesses an enterprise needs to improve.

In a recent development, the difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data. An individual failure tells us something, but training a model requires many new tasks that exercise the same capability in different situations. Those tasks must also be possible to complete in the environment, resemble work someone would actually request, and have a reliable way to check whether the agent succeeded.

It has been revealed that at ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data. It uses a target model’s failures and a stronger teacher’s successes to decide what the model should learn next, then generates and validates fresh tasks that exercise those capabilities. As the model improves, the curriculum shifts toward what it still finds difficult. We illustrate the pipeline with EnterpriseOps Gym (Malay et al., 2026), using the released dataset. We begin by describing the environment an agent operates in and what makes a task useful for training.

An agentic environment defines the world in which an agent operates: the state it can observe and modify, the tools and APIs it can invoke, and the state transitions produced by its actions.

Sources indicate that A task is instantiated within this environment. We use the following abstraction:.

The system specification defines the constraints under which the agent operates, including system instructions, environment policies, and, when applicable, task-specific initialization such as a seeded database state or a set of knowledge articles.

Industry observers note that the specification must be compatible with the environment’s tools, state, and supported actions. Its instructions should be clear and avoid arbitrary constraints introduced solely to manufacture difficulty.

The user prompt specifies what the user wants the agent to accomplish, together with any user-level constraints. A generated task should satisfy three properties.

It has been revealed that feasibility. There should exist at least one trajectory in the current environment that satisfies the user prompt while respecting the system specification. This rules out tasks that depend on unavailable tools, inaccessible knowledge, impossible state transitions, or actions prohibited by policy.

Realism. The user prompt should resemble something a user would plausibly ask in the target environment. The space of executable behaviors is usually much larger than the space of realistic workflows.

In a recent development, difficulty. For training, the task should expose a weakness of the current agent. Tasks that are already solved reliably provide little new training signal. The useful region is therefore tasks that are feasible and realistic, but not yet consistently solved.

According to recent reports, the verifier determines whether the resulting trajectory successfully completes the task. It should satisfy three properties.

In a recent development, consistency. It should agree with the user prompt, the system specification, and the task-specific environment state.

Industry observers note that soundness. It should reject trajectories that fail to satisfy the task or violate relevant constraints.

It has been revealed that completeness. It should accept valid solutions rather than encode one particular reference trajectory.

These properties matter directly during training. A lax verifier can reward incorrect behavior, while an overly restrictive verifier can penalize valid solutions.

Given an environment and a target model, AutoSynthData generates training tasks consisting of a system specification, user prompt, and verifier. The generated tasks are grounded in the environment and selected to provide useful training signal for the current model.

Sources indicate that autoSynthData first evaluates the target model in the environment using diagnostic tasks and identifies patterns in the tasks it struggles to complete. A stronger teacher helps characterize which of those tasks are solvable and what successful behavior looks like. AutoSynthData turns the resulting capability gaps into new executable tasks, checks each task in the environment, and uses accepted samples for post-training. Evaluating the updated model reveals which gaps remain and can guide the next round of generation.

AutoSynthData uses evaluation runs in the target environment to identify what the model needs to learn next. In our EnterpriseOps Gym experiment, we run both the target model and a stronger teacher on the evaluation tasks. We examine those runs to identify:.

We distill these findings into sanitized capability specification cards. The evaluation tasks guide what the model should learn, but the generator does not receive their original prompts, entities, trajectories, or verifier details. It receives the cards and uses them to create latest tasks with different prompts, states, and solution paths.

Identifying a capability gap tells us what to teach, but training requires many varied tasks that exercise it. AutoSynthData uses the specification card to generate those tasks.

Suppose the target model struggles with tasks that require the following workflow:.

It has been revealed that the generator creates fresh tasks that exercise this workflow, varying the entities, initial environment state, workflow composition, tool combinations, wording, and difficulty. The stronger teacher then demonstrates a successful trajectory for each task. For supervised fine-tuning (SFT), these demonstrations teach the target model how to apply the capability in new situations.

AutoSynthData builds the dataset in two phases: first generating and validating core samples, then expanding them into novel variants.

Industry observers note that the target phase creates the core set of training samples from the capability specifications. Workers generate independent tasks in parallel, picking up a fresh target when they finish. Each candidate goes through validation, execution, solver evaluation, and repair before acceptance. The result is a batch of vetted examples built around what the target model needs to learn.

According to recent reports, the multiply phase expands the dataset by creating novel variants of accepted target samples. Each variant has its own user request, environment state, entity configuration, reference trajectory, and verifier, and must pass the same validation and execution checks. A multiplied sample cannot seed another multiplied sample. This anchors expansion to the vetted target set and limits drift across generations.

To support both phases, AutoSynthData separates generation control from environment-specific execution. A shared controller coordinates generation, quality control, coverage, and dataset construction, while an adapter handles environment execution, task and state management, reference replay, deterministic verification, solver execution, and task profiling.

Recent findings suggest that together, parallel target generation and multiplication provide a path to training-scale datasets. Their usefulness depends on the checks applied to every candidate: the task must be executable, the solution must work, and the verifier must distinguish success from failure.

It has been revealed that generating a plausible request is not enough to produce useful training data. A task may be impossible in the target environment, its reference solution may fail when executed, or its verifier may reward the wrong final state. AutoSynthData checks these properties before accepting a task for training.

AutoSynthData reviews quality at two levels: individual candidates must pass verification, and batches must provide useful coverage and diversity.

Industry observers note that each candidate must clear a quality-control loop before entering the training dataset. We begin with solver evaluation to measure difficulty. In the configuration used here, we favor tasks the target model solves on no more than one of three trials and the stronger solver solves on at least two of three trials. Candidates also undergo positive and negative verification and a bounded repair process.

The positive gate asks: Does the intended solution solve the generated task?

It has been revealed that the pipeline executes the reference trajectory in the target environment and checks the resulting state against the candidate’s verifier. This reveals mismatches among the prompt, initial state, solution, and success criteria.

The negative gate asks: Do relevant incorrect outcomes fail?

For example, it can mutate parts of the expected outcome and confirm that those states no longer pass verification. This catches weak verifiers that award success without requiring the intended behavior.

Failed candidates go to a critic before being discarded. The critic examines the sample and its failure, looking for inconsistent state, impossible workflows, incorrect task construction, bad reference trajectories, weak verifier logic, or a mismatch with the intended capability. The critic’s findings guide repairs, with a fixed limit on retries:.

It has been revealed that A repaired task must pass the relevant checks again. The diagnosis guides repairs to the existing candidate rather than requiring generation to start over.

Passing these checks makes a sample eligible for training, but individually valid samples can still form a repetitive or unbalanced dataset. AutoSynthData therefore also reviews generation at the batch level.

A batch may overrepresent a few easy task families, miss a capability, or reflect too much generation effort spent on a low-yield pattern.

A meta-review examines accepted samples, rejected samples, and generation behavior across each batch. It asks:.

The controller tracks coverage in the accepted dataset, reduces generation in overrepresented regions, and directs more work toward gaps. When a region repeatedly produces poor candidates, critiques and meta-review guide changes to the generation strategy. These adjustments balance useful learning signal, task quality, coverage, diversity, and low redundancy within the available generation budget and dataset size requirements.

Together, these feedback loops improve both individual tasks and the dataset they form: sample-level checks guide candidate repair, while batch-level review guides future generation.

In a recent development, the useful training distribution changes as the model improves. AutoSynthData treats synthetic data generation as a search for tasks near the target model's capability boundary: difficult enough to expose weaknesses, but solvable enough for the teacher to provide reliable demonstrations.

Industry observers note that after post-training, we evaluate the updated model in the same environment. Tasks it now solves reliably are less useful for the next training round; persistent failures point to capabilities that still need attention. Those results can guide the next generation round.

Our experiments focus on SFT, but the same mechanism could support reinforcement learning (RL): generate tasks that challenge the current policy and provide reliable learning signal, train, then move the generation target with the updated policy. We proposal to test this moving, difficulty-calibrated frontier beyond SFT.

In a recent development, we use EnterpriseOps Gym to test whether this approach improves a model on tasks in a stateful enterprise environment. We generate training tasks in the Gym’s Hybrid and ITSM environments, fine-tune the target model on accepted samples, and evaluate the resulting checkpoints.

We tested the pipeline on the Hybrid domain of EnterpriseOps Gym using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and Qwen3.8-27B as the teacher.

AutoSynthData generated 2,000 synthetic training samples in about 18 hours. We fine-tuned Gemma on this dataset and evaluated the resulting checkpoints on the benchmark. The best checkpoint was epoch 5.

The synthetic SFT checkpoint improves mean Pass@1 by 7.2 percentage points, a 35% relative improvement, and raises verifier success from 63.01% to 68.55%. It closes 59% of the original Pass@1 gap between Gemma and the reference model.

In a recent development, the training tasks were newly generated from capability specifications; the generator did not receive the original evaluation tasks. The result demonstrates improvement in EnterpriseOps Gym Hybrid, the environment used for this experiment.

It has been revealed that we also applied AutoSynthData to the ITSM domain of EnterpriseOps Gym, using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as the teacher. AutoSynthData generated 1,994 synthetic training samples in 66 hours. Generation took longer than in the subsequent Hybrid run described above, primarily because the ITSM run used a larger teacher model and preceded pipeline optimizations that improved throughput.

On ITSM, synthetic SFT raises mean Pass@1 from 18.77% to 27.18%, showing that the approach also improves performance in a second domain.

Sources indicate that the tasks most useful for training depend on both the environment and the model working in it. AutoSynthData uses the model’s failures to choose what to generate, validates fresh tasks against the environment, and makes those tasks available for post-training. Our EnterpriseOps Gym results show the value of that approach in a controlled setting. As the model changes, the same process can focus on the gaps that remain.

How LinkedIn Built a View-Agnostic Analytics System for Modern iOS UI Architectures

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Nov 23, 2026 2 min read.
  • To address the challenge posed by modern iOS UI systems where the logical UI structure may not mirror the native UIKit hierarchy, LinkedIn engineers developed a view-agnostic analytics system build around a shared MeasurableNode contract.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News How LinkedIn Built a View-Agnostic Analytics System for Modern iOS UI Architectures.

Nov 23, 2026 2 min read.

To address the challenge posed by modern iOS UI systems where the logical UI structure may not mirror the native UIKit hierarchy, LinkedIn engineers developed a view-agnostic analytics system build around a shared MeasurableNode contract.

Recent findings suggest that as LinkedIn senior software engineer Keerthana Reddy Ragi explains, while traditional iOS analytics relies on UIView instances as the unit of measurement, modern UI architectures increasingly use flattened layouts and custom rendering systems where UI elements such as cards, sections, and containers are represented by virtual nodes that never materialize as UIViews. Consequently, analytics systems built solely around UIKit may fail to capture impressions for virtual nodes, lose logical hierarchy and contextual information, miscalculate visibility and impression duration, and attribute user actions to the wrong elements.

Sources indicate that linkedIn's solution introduces a shared MeasurableNode contract relaxing the requirement for every measurable element to be a UIView. A MeasurableNode exposes four properties: identity, geometry, hierarchy, and lifecycle.

As MeasurableNode is a shared contract, both traditional UIViews and virtual nodes can participate in the same analytics system. Indeed, while existing UIKit views continue using native UIKit properties and lifecycle hooks, virtual nodes explicitly provide the corresponding information to the same analytics layer.

It has been revealed that the attach and detach methods are central to this approach, because they enable the layout or rendering system to notify the analytics system "when a node attaches, when its frame changes, and when it detaches". Unlike virtual nodes, UIKit already sends automatic lifecycle notifications to UIViews. Similarly, as virtual nodes are not directly recognized by UIKit as gesture-recognizer targets, the rendering framework must traverse the hybrid UIKit/virtual-node parent hierarchy to attribute user actions to the appropriate logical virtual node.

Ragi emphasizes that this design enables gradual adoption without requiring existing view-based analytics to be rewritten.

Sources indicate that teams can modernize one part of the UI without rewriting everything around it. Existing view-based analytics can keep working while newer virtual nodes use the new contract.

In a recent development, linkedIn engineers encountered three main challenges developing this approach to analytics. First, the widespread assumption that everything is a UIView is embedded in existing codebases. For example, "helper code that walked superviews, visibility checks that read frames directly from views, cleanup logic tied to view removal". All these cases had to be found and updated. Second, they had to strike the right balance between short-term compatibility and long-term correctness. Third, they needed to enforce the attach/detach discipline at the framework level.

Commenting on Ragi's article on LinkedIn, senior AI prompt engineer Artien Nadal observed:.

Recent findings suggest that I think there's a bigger opportunity here than just making analytics independent of the UI. What if teams could automatically detect when a UI change breaks event tracking or changes what an event actually means?

In a recent development, as a final note, although LinkedIn's implementation focused on UIKit, the underlying approach is far from being limited to it. With many apps now mixing UIKit and SwiftUI, cross-platform layout engines, or hybrid solutions, a view-agnostic analytics model based on a shared contract has broader applicability.

#116097. Beyond Linux: A Journey Through the Open Source Ecosystem

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 24m • 📚 Deep Dive (4774 w)

Beyond Linux: A Journey Through the Open Source Ecosystem

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4774 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dragas

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that what follows is the text of the talk I gave at Linux Day 2026 in Modena, lightly adapted for the blog.
  • Recent findings suggest that linux is one of the best-known players in the open source world, but it's not the only possible path.
  • According to recent reports, my name is Stefano Marinelli.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that what follows is the text of the talk I gave at Linux Day 2026 in Modena, lightly adapted for the blog. The talk was in Italian, in front of a Linux audience - which explains a few of the jokes.

Recent findings suggest that linux is one of the best-known players in the open source world, but it's not the only possible path. A journey through the BSDs, illumos and other alternative operating systems, to reflect on Open Source as an idea, a philosophy and a practice of sharing knowledge.

According to recent reports, my name is Stefano Marinelli. I'm a sysadmin and consultant, and I run my own small firm specialised in open source services and solutions. I like to call myself the "Barista" of the BSD Cafe and the illumos Cafe, online communities of people passionate about technology, open source and sharing. Today I'm not here just to talk about operating systems, but about freedom, sharing and knowledge. From free software to open source.

My first contact with the Free Software world was in 1996, when I wasn't even 17 yet. I saw a box set advertised in a magazine: "a whole operating system, for free", at a very low price. Something like 30,000 lire. Shortly before, I'd paid roughly ten times as much for the Windows 95 upgrade edition. Dismissive and without a shred of trust, I decided to order it and give it a go. I mean: who would ever write something like that... and release the source code? But six CDs for 30,000 lire... let's try. Worst case, it'll be an experience.

It was love at first shell. That terminal opened up a whole universe, and to what I already knew (commercial licences, freeware, shareware) I added the concept of Free Software. But I didn't have enough hardware to run two operating systems, so I reinstalled Windows and put it all off. Still, I started thinking. Reflecting. Studying. In 1997 I got a fresh PC and started using Linux - or, as I was careful to say, GNU/Linux - for everything. Except games. For those, a small Windows partition survived, though not for long.

In 1998 I enrolled in Computer Science at the University of Bologna. Even back then, it was a faculty strongly oriented towards free software. Linux in the labs. I was one of the few who, in the first year, already knew what Free Software was (not free as in price, but...freedom!) and how to use the Linux workstations. That gave me a big advantage, especially from the second year onwards. Renzo Davoli was already pushing hard in that direction. I decided that would be my path. And so it was, and I started pushing too. Windows wasn't the "enemy" to me. The imposition was. Personally, I respect rules, but not impositions. Some people followed me, others watched from a distance. I didn't care. I was widening my horizons.

Industry observers note that in the early 2000s I also discovered the BSDs. And I convinced my parents that I needed a laser printer for "university material". In reality, I wanted to print the excellent BSD documentation. Maybe not university material, but the printed FreeBSD Handbook probably served me better than half of the theory exams I took back then. Thanks, mom and dad!

But let's get back to the beginning.

Free Software was born out of a change. In those days, code circulated freely among people. Depending on their needs, they exchanged source code, modified it and shared it again. But at some point this began to change. There's an anecdote that, while not exhaustive, gives the idea: the printer Richard Stallman was using kept jamming, and nobody got notified. He wanted to modify the software so that he'd get a notification, as he'd done with the previous printer. Back then it was common practice, but this time he was refused. "I can't share the source code. It's under NDA." In other words, he had lost control over what he was using. He even wanted to improve the program, and instead he got a refusal.

In a recent development, the rest is history. At least until a few years ago.

It has been revealed that because thirty years ago we fought for Free Software to be taken seriously. When I started working, I was almost laughed at. "That's toy stuff you use at university. The real world uses something else." "Why don't you just use Windows? Everything's easier." And yet, the toys often worked better than the expensive proprietary solutions. Or at least just as well, at a fraction of the cost. "Let's try. Don't pay me until you're satisfied." They smiled, incredulous. Then they paid, happily. We could prove there was an alternative. Free, with no artificial locks. Something that anyone - even the broke but eager student - could study and set up. Technology, that kind of "enterprise" technology, was truly within everyone's reach. There was no need to buy expensive products, or recurring certifications just to have the "right" to work on them. You study, you apply yourself, nobody can stop you. I attended Linux Days. I spoke at Linux Days. For example, here I am, in Linux Day 2004.

Recent findings suggest that we won that battle. We won that war. Linux - chaotic Linux, built by countless external contributors, made of different and varied distributions - has reached everywhere. Open Source is everywhere. But something happened - something beautiful, but terrible: precisely because it reached everywhere, something changed in the spirit. "Too major to fail". And so the big players arrived. Today, Linux development is driven by corporate money: companies like Microsoft (the same Microsoft that once considered Linux its sworn enemy - or Red Hat itself) and other big tech players. In itself, this has been a good thing. In practice, though, it means that they steer its development, even if indirectly. Year after year, it has started to take the shape of a different kind of product. Is the user still at the centre, or is it more code to make Azure run better? Sure, it's Open Source, it's free. But it's increasingly close to the needs of the big companies funding its development and, at times, further from the ordinary user. That's not necessarily bad: many of these investments have given us extraordinary technologies.

Sources indicate that but I wonder whether, in the process, we're losing something. Not so much in the code as in the mindset. If not in the kernel, then in the community around it.

Back then, precisely because we were frustrated by "It only works on Windows", we were careful to write portable software. I'll say one word, without going into too much detail: POSIX. Once a mantra: POSIX compliant. A set of standards defining common interfaces between operating systems, so you can write programs that, with few or even no changes, run on different Unix and Unix-like systems. Today, in the communities around Linux, you hear more and more often that POSIX is "outdated". When I send a patch to make a specific tool work on FreeBSD, for example, I often read comments like: "Why don't you just use Linux?". And that dÃ©jÃ  vu sends a shiver down my spine: is the community I loved so much turning into a copy, albeit a better one, of its worst enemy?

Industry observers note that but careful: I'm not here to speak ill of Linux. That would be absurd. I mean: coming to Linux Day to trash Linux? It's an extraordinary operating system, and I owe it a great deal.

I'm here to remind you that Linux isn't the only way to understand free software. And that a project being less well known doesn't make it less interesting, less valid or less worthy of attention. Because if freedom of choice is truly a value, we must be ready to defend it even when someone chooses something different from what we choose.

So let's see what lies beyond Linux. Because monoculture is a problem, in Open Source too.

Because free software is...free. And we must be free too. Free to choose, to consider alternatives. To contribute, if we want to. To understand which solution best fits our problem. We don't have to pick a single solution "because everyone does". We don't have to turn one monopoly into another. Linux is great. It helps put bread on my table, so I'm a fan. But there are alternatives, other solutions, that can have their advantages. And that's why I want to talk to you about the BSDs and illumos.

Sources indicate that BSD stands for Berkeley Software Distribution. And the first curious thing is that its story begins before Linux even existed. We're in the late Seventies. At the University of California, Berkeley, some researchers are working on UNIX, the operating system developed at AT&T's Bell Labs. They don't just use it. They modify it, improve it, write fresh programs and share that work with other universities.

It has been revealed that remind you of something? We've just been talking about Stallman and the culture of sharing.

Industry observers note that BSD was born in exactly that world. So it was born on solid, stable, reliable foundations. Studied by experts, not as a game. BSD was an operating system directly related to Unix. It was a complete and stable system, but it wasn't yet available for "home" systems, the i386 family. Born well before Linux. A curiosity: Linus Torvalds himself, in a 1993 interview, stated: "If 386BSD had been available when I started on Linux, Linux would probably never had happened.". Yes, you heard that right. Linus Torvalds said it. And we're at a Linux Day!

Then something happened: BSD arrived on the i386, and Unix System Laboratories, controlled by AT&T, started a rather insidious legal dispute: there's our code in BSD and you have no right to use, modify or share it. The University of California was dragged into it too. This was a real blocker for many. Companies were afraid to adopt an operating system with a lawsuit like that in progress. The matter dragged on until 1994, when a settlement was reached and 4.4BSD-Lite was released, with a freely redistributable and legally cleared base.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, Linux was growing, attracting developers, winning users. It didn't have that particular legal uncertainty. I'm not saying Linux succeeded only because of this. That would be unfair to Torvalds and to the thousands of people who contributed to its development.

Recent findings suggest that but it's interesting to think that the history of computing as we know it could have taken a different path. And it's also interesting that, despite these difficulties, BSD didn't disappear. Quite the opposite.

From that story came some of the operating systems I want to talk about today. Systems that took different paths and that are still developed, used and improved. Different operating systems - careful, not distributions of the same operating system! - each unique in its own way. Let's start with FreeBSD.

FreeBSD is probably the most general-purpose BSD. It's a complete operating system, designed to offer stability, performance and a certain consistency in administration. And here's a first difference from Linux I'd like to highlight. In the BSDs, the kernel and the userland, the base tools of the operating system, are developed and maintained within the same project. That doesn't mean Linux works worse. It means the development model is different.

Industry observers note that and there's a philosophy I really appreciate: evolution, not revolution. It doesn't mean standing still. It means trying to improve without necessarily turning upside down what already works.

Recent findings suggest that let's talk about some technologies. ZFS, for example. An advanced filesystem, with snapshots, data integrity, replication and many other features. FreeBSD integrates it directly into the system and also lets you use Boot Environments: I can upgrade the system and, if something goes wrong, go back to the previous environment.

Then we have jails. FreeBSD has had a technology for isolating processes, resources and application environments since 2000. Long before Docker arrived. Jails aren't Docker, and I'm not saying they're the same thing. But they let you isolate applications and services simply, with low overhead, using the operating system's own features directly. A bit like LXC on Linux.

According to recent reports, for virtualisation we have bhyve, which lets you run virtual machines, including other operating systems. And bhyve is lighter and, often, faster than KVM on Linux. [LINK: my bhyve articles].

According to recent reports, but FreeBSD isn't just a system for enthusiasts. Netflix uses it to deliver video content. PlayStation consoles have a FreeBSD-derived base. macOS and iOS also include code from the BSD world. OPNsense and pfSense, two well-known firewall solutions, are based on FreeBSD. In short, we're not talking about a university toy. Remind you of something?

Personally, I've been using FreeBSD for many years, in production too. And it has often let me solve problems simply, while staying in control of what's happening. I've seen cases where, on the same hardware and with the same workload, FreeBSD handled I/O pressure better, with even very significant reductions in execution time. If you're curious, there are several articles about it here on IT Notes. That doesn't mean FreeBSD is always faster than Linux. That would be nonsense. It means there are situations where it can be the better choice.

Sources indicate that and for me, this is the point: I solve problems. I don't have to defend an operating system. I have to pick the right tool.

Then there's OpenBSD. OpenBSD was born in 1995 as a fork of NetBSD and is probably one of the most interesting systems when we talk about security and code correctness.

Recent findings suggest that its philosophy is fairly simple: less complexity, fewer chances for mistakes. The code is continuously reviewed, cleaned up, simplified. Features aren't added just because they might be interesting. Every choice has to make sense within the project. Because the more complex code becomes, the harder it is to maintain, audit and verify.

OpenBSD has also developed some very interesting security mechanisms, like pledge() and unveil(), which let you restrict the operations a program can perform and the parts of the filesystem it can access.

And then there's OpenSSH. Yes, the very OpenSSH you probably use every day to manage your servers. It was born, and is developed, within the OpenBSD project.

But there's another feature I love: the documentation. In the OpenBSD world, insufficient or wrong documentation is considered a bug. The man pages are often enough to understand how to use and configure the system, without hunting for guides of dubious quality scattered across the Internet. And believe me, when you manage dozens or hundreds of systems, knowing where to find correct and consistent information is a huge advantage.

According to recent reports, openBSD doesn't try to please everyone. The developers follow their own priorities, even when that means giving up something other systems offer. Can it be frustrating? Certainly. But it also offers a great advantage: consistency, predictability and a clear design direction.

For firewalls, routers and systems where security is particularly important, it's an alternative always worth considering.

It has been revealed that netBSD, on the other hand, has a wonderful motto. "Of course it runs NetBSD!" And that already claims a lot about its philosophy.

Recent findings suggest that netBSD puts a huge emphasis on portability, correctness of implementation and the ability to run on very different hardware architectures. Not just modern x86 or ARM computers. We're also talking about machines decades old, architectures many consider long forgotten. And careful: it's not just a matter of computing nostalgia.

Keeping an operating system working on such different platforms forces you to write code with great attention to portability, avoiding needless dependencies on a specific architecture.

Remember when, a moment ago, I was talking about POSIX and portability as a value? Well, NetBSD is one of the best examples of that philosophy. Because a system that can run on very different hardware must necessarily care about how correct, clean and portable its code is. And that has positive consequences on the more common platforms too.

There's another aspect I appreciate: continuity. We don't always need the latest novelty, the latest feature, the latest framework. Some devices and applications simply need to keep working, maybe for many years. Think of embedded systems, small computers, hardware that isn't replaced every two years. In these contexts, knowing there's a project that considers portability and support for different architectures a fundamental part of its identity is reassuring.

It's a different philosophy from FreeBSD's and from OpenBSD's. And that's absolutely fine.

NetBSD has also taken a clear stance on AI-generated code: it can't be committed without prior written approval, because it's considered potentially "tainted" - both in form and in licence. And in today's extremely polarised world, that's a sigh of relief for anyone who wants to use and develop an operating system without the pressure of always having to do more, add more features and more code.

There's also DragonFlyBSD, born in 2003 as a fork of FreeBSD, which followed other design choices, especially regarding the kernel and system management. We don't have time to go into everything, but I want to stress one thing. These systems have common origins and share part of their history, but they don't necessarily have the same goals.

FreeBSD is a general-purpose system, also oriented towards performance and production environments. It's stable and secure. On the desktop it might not support all the hardware Linux does, although they're working on it. But on servers it could be one of the best alternatives to Linux.

It has been revealed that openBSD favours security, simplicity and code correctness. NetBSD focuses heavily on portability and on supporting different hardware. DragonFlyBSD has experimented with other architectural solutions. And yet, they all belong to the substantial BSD family.

It has been revealed that there's no need for one to win over the others. It's not a battle. There's nothing to sell here. It's freedom. It's diversity. And that diversity is a strength.

According to recent reports, if there's one thing I've learnt over all these years, it's exactly this: an operating system shouldn't be a religion. In my daily life, I solve problems. And to solve them, I need to be able to evaluate the alternatives.

Because stability, for example, isn't just a system's ability not to crash. It's also being able to enhancement it without surprises, to understand how it works, to know what happens when something goes wrong. Observability is fundamental, and being able to have it without weaving together fifty Docker containers can sometimes make the difference between ten minutes of work and two hours.

In a recent development, we don't always need to reinvent everything. What's new isn't always better. And the solution chosen by the majority isn't always the best fit for our problem. Often, it's exactly the opposite.

But our journey doesn't end with the BSDs.

It has been revealed that there's another family of operating systems that descends from a different UNIX history. A history that runs through Sun Microsystems, Solaris and OpenSolaris. And that leads us to illumos.

Now someone might ask: weren't you talking about the BSDs? Yes, but the talk is called Beyond Linux, not Only BSD!

illumos isn't a BSD. It descends from another branch of the big UNIX family. The Solaris one, developed by Sun Microsystems. Sun. Anyone remember it? SPARC workstations, servers, Solaris, Java. In the Nineties and the 2000s it was one of the biggest names in professional computing.

And Solaris was a very interesting operating system. Designed for serious machines, serious workloads, situations where a problem could cost a lot. In Bologna, when I was a student, there were some Solaris machines in the UnderLab. I looked at them sideways. To me they were "non-Linux". So I didn't like them.

Recent findings suggest that in 2005 Sun did something significant: it started publishing the Solaris source code through the OpenSolaris project. Imagine: a commercial UNIX system, with years of development behind it, advanced technologies and long experience in enterprise environments, opening up to the community. It wasn't the first free software to be used in companies, of course. But it was another way of doing things. Another model.

And then, in 2010, Oracle acquired Sun. And here things changed. Oracle decided to stop the open development of OpenSolaris and stopped publishing upcoming code updates.

It has been revealed that because the code that had already been released under an open source licence remained available. Oracle could decide not to publish its developments any more, but it couldn't take back the freedoms already granted on that code. And that's how illumos was born. A group of developers decided to carry on the work, starting from the open OpenSolaris base.

Think about it for a moment. A company acquires another company, changes strategy and stops the public development of an operating system. But that system doesn't die. Because the code exists, the skills exist, and there are people willing to keep working on it.

Remind you of something? We began this talk with Stallman and a printer whose code couldn't be shared. Thirty years later, the very possibility of sharing and modifying code allows a whole family of operating systems to keep existing.

This, for me, is one of the most beautiful aspects of free software.

According to recent reports, but let's get back to the technology. Because illumos isn't just a nice story.

Industry observers note that from Solaris, illumos inherited some extremely interesting technologies. You already know one: ZFS. ZFS was born at Sun. It's a filesystem, but also a volume manager. It lets you manage storage, snapshots, data replication, integrity checks and much more.

Recent findings suggest that I use ZFS practically everywhere I can. On FreeBSD, on illumos, on NetBSD and on Linux too. And that's already an example of how a good technology can cross different operating systems.

Then we have DTrace. DTrace lets you observe what's happening inside a system, even while it's running. We can analyse kernel calls, processes, performance, behaviours that would otherwise be hard to understand. For a sysadmin, it's an extraordinary tool. Because when a client tells you "the server is slow", the problem isn't knowing it's slow. They already know that. The problem is understanding why.

According to recent reports, then there are Zones. An isolation system that lets you run separate environments sharing the same kernel. Remember FreeBSD's jails? Well, zones were inspired by FreeBSD's jails. The concept is similar, although the implementations and some features differ.

And then Crossbow, for network virtualisation. SMF, for managing services and their dependencies. In short, we're talking about a system with notable technologies, born to tackle concrete problems. Not an experiment cobbled together in someone's spare time. And careful, I'm not saying these technologies are necessarily better than those available on Linux or the BSDs. I'm saying they're different, they have their own history and, in certain contexts, they can be particularly useful.

Like Linux, illumos is the base of several distributions, each with different features and goals.

In a recent development, smartOS, for example, is focused on virtualisation. It has an interesting peculiarity: the operating system is loaded into RAM, from USB or from the network (or even from the local disk, but then it runs read-only), leaving the disks to the virtual machines and the data, managed with ZFS. It supports native Zones, LX zones to run Linux applications, and virtual machines via KVM and bhyve. Yes, the very bhyve we've already met talking about FreeBSD! Personally, I'm using and experimenting with it a lot. It's not all roses, but I really like some of its solutions. And bhyve on illumos even has a few gems that haven't been brought back to FreeBSD. Open Source and collaboration between projects, at their best!

Sources indicate that omniOS takes a more traditional road. It's an operating system designed mainly for servers, with particular attention to stability, updates and long-term continuity. It offers stable releases and long-term support versions. You install it, configure your services and use it. Without necessarily having to reinvent everything at every revision.

OpenIndiana is perhaps the closest to the classic idea of a general-purpose UNIX distribution. It can be used on servers, but also as a desktop system, with a full graphical environment. For anyone who'd like to try a Solaris-derived system on their own computer, it could be an interesting starting point.

Recent findings suggest that and then there's Tribblix, a rather special project. Created by Peter Tribble, it combines an almost nostalgic, traditional UNIX feel with modern components. It has its own package management system and a modular approach through overlays, which let you install groups of software. A small, independent system with a very precise personality.

Recent findings suggest that four distributions sharing a technological base, but interpreting it in different ways. Remind you of something? Linux... And that's exactly the point. There's no single way to build an operating system. There's no single development philosophy.

Industry observers note that and none of them needs to prevail over the others. What matters is that they keep existing, evolving and offering alternatives. Because, in the end, freedom of choice only has value if we really have something to choose from.

Industry observers note that because there's a whole UNIX tradition that isn't Linux and isn't BSD. Because some technologies now considered fundamental in modern computing were born right there. And, still today, they're stable and reliable. They're refined and polished without being "rewritten" or replaced every five years because there's a new fashion. Because we can use systems that followed different paths, with different architectures and design choices.

But above all, because illumos is also a practical demonstration of the value of free software. Sun opened the code. Oracle decided to stop that open development. The community was able to carry on.

It wasn't easy, and it doesn't mean every open source project can automatically survive the disappearance of whoever was funding it. You need developers, resources, skills. You need someone willing to take care of it. Available code is a necessary condition, but on its own it isn't enough.

Industry observers note that and this brings us to a point that, for me, is fundamental. Free software isn't just code. It's also the people who choose to develop it, maintain it, document it and share it.

That's why, alongside the BSD Cafe, I also wanted to create the illumos Cafe. To offer a space to meet, discuss and share experiences about technologies that maybe don't make the front pages of tech sites every day.

According to recent reports, because we don't all have to use the same operating system. We don't even all have to agree. But we can learn something from each other. And maybe discover a solution to a problem we didn't even know we could tackle differently.

Careful, though. I'm not saying the BSD or illumos communities are better than the Linux ones. In our world too there's fundamentalism, prejudice, and people who consider their own choice the only possible one. And that's a problem too. Because it makes no sense to defend software freedom and then look down on someone who decides to use a system different from ours.

Sources indicate that we don't all have to agree. In fact, it would be terribly boring. We must be able to disagree, compare ideas, learn something and keep respecting each other - even in disagreement - while building something constructive. What matters, in the end, is being able to choose. And that's true freedom.

In a recent development, more than twenty years ago, at Linux Days, I talked about how Linux could replace Windows in many areas, both on the desktop and on servers. That it was a valid alternative. Today I'm here to tell you not to let yourselves be chained by habit. Linux/Docker/Kubernetes is an exceptional combination, but not the only one. It would be serious if it were, because we'd have lost our freedom. The freedom to publish an Open Source project as a tarball of source code instead of putting it "on GitHub" or similar.

Open source is not about doing things the approved way. It is about giving people the freedom to do things another way.

Open Source and Closed Minds never get along.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kristof Beyls has published a summary to the LLVM discussion forum to announce that the project is declaring success and bringing its relicensing effort to a close after eight years.
  • We've been asking past contributors to relicense their work since 2018.
  • It has been revealed that rather than trying to "chase the last tiny fraction forever" LLVM is winding up the effort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kristof Beyls has published a summary to the LLVM discussion forum to announce that the project is declaring success and bringing its relicensing effort to a close after eight years.

We've been asking past contributors to relicense their work since 2018. Upcoming contributions have come in under Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception since January 19, 2019. Code contributed before that date was under LLVM's earlier licenses (UIUC/NCSA, plus MIT for some runtime libraries), so we needed permission from its authors to move it over. [...].

It has been revealed that rather than trying to "chase the last tiny fraction forever" LLVM is winding up the effort. Any contributors with code contributed before January 19, 2019 who have not signed a relicensing agreement and do not want their contributions made available under Apache-2.0 with the LLVM-exception can still reach out to the project to ensure their code has the appropriate SPDX license identifier.

Note: you can avoid this step in the future by logging into your LWN account.

The Agent Remarked It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.

📅 03 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2586 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row.
  • Sources indicate that figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind.
  • Sources indicate that A customer writes in.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row. It is now available through Hugging Face.

Sources indicate that figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind. From our ThinkingBox paper.

Sources indicate that A customer writes in. Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.

Industry observers note that the AI agent does careful work. Nine tool calls: it pulls the order, checks tracking, looks up her customer profile, searches the refund policy twice, confirms no ticket exists, opens one, documents the timeline, and reads the policy correctly; her account segment genuinely does not qualify for late-delivery compensation.

Industry observers note that then it closes the ticket as resolved and replies “ Since your query is resolved, is there anything I may assist you with? ”.

Sources indicate that two things are wrong. The carrier exception is still open, so the required end state was on hold, pending resolution. And the customer never got a real answer to what she actually asked.

In a recent development, an AI grader checking tool calls would see nine well-formed ones. The grader checking whether the agent wrote to the database would see that too. The database is what disagrees.

That gap is what ThinkingBox measures. Across 507 stateful business workflows, each run 20 times against various LLM models, it grades agents on terminal backend state and side effects. This post covers what we found, what consistency costs, and how to run the benchmark yourself through OpenEnv.

You can run this one yourself: the example above is adapted from a benchmark task sandbox_external_retail_group1.py:test_case_ST003_006, and the executable check that fails is a single field: the ticket's status is solved where the required end state is hold. The full trace is in Appendix D.4, Case 3 of our paper.

Want to try it before reading the results? Skip to section Run it yourself.

Final responses and valid tool calls are only proxies. An agent can sound correct while leaving the wrong value, changing the wrong record, or creating an extra side effect. Only the records it leaves behind settle the question.

The gap is substantial. In a common-set ablation covering 121,680 valid trials across 12 LLM models, 79,853 attempts failed the executable checks. Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error. Executable checks nevertheless found wrong field values in 77.61% of them, unintended extra effects in 43.30%, and missing required effects in 25.36%. Those state-check findings overlap.

According to recent reports, A trajectory is a claim. Database state is the evidence. Repetition is the trust test.

An agent that processes a refund correctly once and mishandles it the next four times is not a working refund agent. So every task runs 20 independent times, each from an identical clean backend, and we report three different things:.

Table 1: The three numbers we report, and the question each one answers.

We use observed 20/20 in this blog post as the literal count of how many of the 507 tasks passed 20 out of 20. No estimator, no smoothing.

Starting with the familiar view. The table below reports pass@1, the single-attempt score estimate, broken out by domain. This is the number most leaderboards publish, and on its own it reads like an ordinary capability ranking.

It has been revealed that table 2: ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain. Each model is evaluated on every task for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the group leader; underline marks the runner-up. The standard errors for the single attempt score estimates are provided in Table 4 in our ThinkingBox paper.

According to recent reports, claude Opus 5.5 leads overall at 67.16%, two-thirds of a point above Claude Opus 5. Kimi-K3 is the strongest open-weights model, within a point of GPT-6-Astra. Domain matters just as much: Claude Opus 4.6 scores 68.62% on retail but 8.30% on auto insurance.

One good run tells you a model can do the work. It does not tell you whether it will do it again. So run every task 20 times and ask how much of that score survives.

Figure 2: How much of each model's single-attempt score survives 20 repeats.

Sources indicate that only three hold on to most of their pass@1 scores: GPT-6 Astra retains 78% of its single-attempt rate, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Opus 5 each retain 71%. At the other end, GLM-5.1, Kimi-K2.6 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro each keep about 8%.

The gap between what a model can do once and what it does every time is the whole story.

Industry observers note that figure 3: Breadth and consistency pull apart. Twelve of the eighteen models are shown; six below 33% pass@1 are omitted for legibility.

Kimi-K3 has the broadest coverage of any model we tested. It solves 93.89% of the benchmark at least once: 476 of 507 tasks. Only 31 tasks defeat it entirely, the lowest count in the field. On retail workflows it leads outright at 82.24% pass@1, ahead of every proprietary model.

Sources indicate that kimi-K3 is also among the least consistent. Just 68 of 507 tasks, 13.41%, succeed in all 20 attempts.

It has been revealed that claude Opus 5 inverts this. It solves fewer tasks at least once (79.09%; 106 defeat it entirely) but completes 47.53% of the benchmark on every single attempt.

Recent findings suggest that A newer model does not fix this. Claude Opus 5.5 scores higher than Claude Opus 5 on every-attempt average, 67.16% against 66.50%, and solves more tasks at least once. It passes exactly the same number of tasks on all 20 attempts: 241. Half a point of headline accuracy bought no additional dependability at all.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches real records, pass@20 is the wrong column to look at.

Capability comparisons usually stop at the score. For anyone deploying, the relevant question is what a successful unit of work costs. We measure that as cost per successful task attempt. We say task attempt because every benchmark task is run repeatedly and cost is incurred per attempt, so pass@1 is the matching quality denominator.

We took each model's recorded token usage from its full 507 × 20 campaign and priced it at undiscounted list rates available on OpenRouter+, reversing promotional discounts and excluding endpoints that declare quantization. Input, output and cache rates all come from one provider endpoint per model.

Then we divided one run's cost by the number of attempts that succeeded:.

Cost per successful task attempt = estimated cost for 507 attempts, one per task ÷ (507 × pass@1).

This is a comparative efficiency index, not an invoice, and not the price of serving one production request. It also prices single successes, not consistency. We price consistency next.

Example: GPT-5.4 costs $43.49 for 507 attempts (one attempt per task) and has 65.36% pass@1, so $43.49 ÷ (507 × 0.6536) = $0.131 per successful task attempt.

A model is on the frontier if no other model is both no more expensive and at least as accurate. Three models qualify; every other model is dominated on at least one axis.

Industry observers note that figure 4: Cost per successful task attempt against pass@1. Ringed dots are pareto cost frontier models.

The frontier has three steps. GPT-5.6 Sol has the lowest cost per success at $0.127; GPT-5.4 raises pass@1 by 3.45 percentage points for $0.004 more per success; Claude Opus 5.5 adds another 1.80 points at $0.276 per success. Each of the three remains on the cost frontier line because no cheaper model matches its pass@1.

Claude Opus 5 is the clearest case: at $0.475 per successful attempt and 66.50% pass@1, it is both more expensive and less accurate than Claude Opus 5.5 at $0.276 and 67.16%.

Cost per success rewards a model that is cheap and often right. It does not reward a model that is right every time. So we also compute cost per dependable task: the cost of the full 20-run campaign divided by the number of tasks the model passed on all 20 attempts.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of 20 runs of 507 attempts ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Example: GPT-6-Astra costs 20 × $86.03 = $1,720.60 for the campaign and passes 231 tasks on every attempt, so $1,720.60 ÷ 231 = $7.45 per dependable task.

Table 3: The nine lowest costs per dependable task among models with at least one observed 20/20 task, sorted low to high. Estimated $, not actual cloud bills.

Now rank by consistency. GPT-5.4 is the cheapest at $6.80, though only 128 tasks meet the bar. GPT-6 Astra reaches 231 at $7.45, and Claude Opus 5.5 the joint-highest 241 at $7.80.

None of the three dominates the others: each additional dependable task costs more. Claude Opus 5 also passes 241, but at $13.30, so Opus 5.5 dominates it outright. GPT-5.6 Sol, the cheapest per single success at $0.127, costs $9.76 per dependable task. The cheapest way to get a right answer is not the cheapest way to get a dependable one.

In a recent development, we assign each failed trace one deterministic diagnostic signature, and the headline is actionable: roughly four in five failures are tool handling, not reasoning. Across an ablation study in Table 5 of our paper:.

These are unweighted averages of per-model shares and observable labels, not unique causal explanations.

In a recent development, the practical pattern is simple: agents usually get far enough to attempt the workflow, then fail to recover from tool errors, failed preconditions, or empty lookups. That is a retry and error-recovery problem before it is a model problem.

Difficulty also changes by domain: across the models listed in Table 2 above, retail averages 59.52% pass@1 while auto insurance averages 33.83%.

What to do about it. Treat the 20/20 rate as a design input, not a verdict. The same signal the benchmark grades on is available in production: check the terminal state before you commit, not the model's summary of it.

Classify tool and system errors so retries target the recoverable ones. Cut the tool surface to what the workflow needs. And require human approval on the changes you cannot cheaply reverse. We have not measured the lift from any of these on this benchmark, which is exactly the kind of thing the environment now makes testable.

ThinkingBox is the agent sandbox, while ThinkingBox-Bench is a dataset benchmark to evaluate agents. The diagram at the top of this post indicates the loop; here is what each part does.

Figure 5: The sandbox loop from panel A in Figure 1 above: isolated tool session, terminal database state, side effects, executable judges.

Recent findings suggest that each task defines a starting backend state, a user goal, the available MCP tools, the domain policy, and executable checks over the terminal state. A simulated user holds private context (a booking reference, a preference, or a date of birth) and releases it only when asked.

Every attempt gets an isolated MCP session with freshly initialized state. Two attempts of the same task never share a database row or cached tool state, which is what makes 20-trial comparison meaningful.

It has been revealed that at the end, a side-effect extractor derives what actually changed, and deterministic judges compare it against the required end state, accepting any trajectory that produces the right outcome while rejecting wrong, missing or extra effects. For requirements with no clean database value ("did the agent disclose this is not guaranteed?"), a narrow binary rubric question handles the semantics. 477 of the 507 tasks are graded on state alone; 30 add response rubrics.

Sources indicate that the trust boundary: the model sees tasks, dialogue and tool schemas. Golden state, assertions, grading internals and credentials stay on the evaluator side.

ThinkingBox is now on Hugging Face, both the harness and the dataset. ThinkingBox-Bench now sits behind the OpenEnv interface, and each finished episode returns a binary pass/fail reward. The released adapter is designed for evaluation; separate, non-benchmark scenarios can use the same interface in training workflows.

Tested on Linux and WSL, with Python 3.11+, uv and Docker. You also need a thinkingbox-data checkout at the pinned release and model endpoints for the agent, simulated user and judge. One endpoint can serve all three roles, which is the simplest way to start. The OpenEnv image starts only the OpenEnv API; everything else you run yourself.

In a second terminal, start Typesense 30.1 and wait for its health check:.

In a third terminal, start the Session Proxy and MCP servers.

Back in the first terminal, start the OpenEnv server against a ThinkingBox YAML config naming your three models (config guide):.

Gate on readiness before running anything. It returns 503 until its observable data, configuration and Session Proxy checks pass. It cannot observe Typesense or live-probe every model endpoint, so confirm those separately:.

Now score a real episode. example_usage.py only resets and lists tools; for agent actions, effects and assertions use the packaged evaluator:.

The OpenEnv adapter writes operational failures to an errors sidecar so they can be rerun rather than silently mixed with model outcomes. A canonical result must resolve or explicitly account for those attempts; we counted system errors as unsuccessful trials.

Runs are gated on a pinned framework commit, a pinned data release and a bundle hash, so a canonical result is verifiable rather than asserted.

Recent findings suggest that the useful part of this work is not our pass@1 leaderboard. It is the environment.

If you are evaluating an agent that touches real records:.

Further details can be found in the following links:.

ThinkingBox code is MIT-licensed; the benchmark data is CDLA-Permissive-2.0; the OpenEnv environment ships under OpenEnv's BSD-3-Clause.

Industry observers note that disclaimer: every task in the public benchmark is a synthetic reconstruction. The workflows and policies are modeled on real AI agentic enterprise patterns; the customers are not real.

According to recent reports, thinkingBox and ThinkingBox-Bench is built by the Microsoft Copilot Studio team in partnership with Toloka with collaborators from the University of Pittsburgh, Northwestern University, Columbia University and UC Irvine who interned at Microsoft. Questions are welcome in the comments section below or on github or by email at firstnamelastname@microsoft.com.

+ OpenRouter cost snapshot taken on Sept 20th 2026; Opus 5.5 pricing as per the Anthropic site.

ST003_006 delegates its pass check to validate_database. Unequal result and golden database hashes fail even when diff is empty. The diff explains a failure; it does not decide the pass.

This small replay exercises the released function with four authored effect inputs. Run python3 reproduce.py. It verifies the source pin and tests supplied hashes; it does not calculate a database hash, run an agent, or reproduce the full environment.

AI-assisted source reading and example by CyberNative AI LLC.

The useful cut is agent-reported "done" versus backend terminal state.

In a recent development, A green success from the same process that acted is a claim, not a grade. I'd want the eval to score durable side effects (ticket status, refund state, policy-cited fields) against a frozen oracle — and fail when the narrative is green while the database disagrees.

Practical check: can a run be marked done when the terminal-state fixture is red?
