💡 Key Takeaways
  • Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%.
  • In a recent development, we’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect.
  • In our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%.

In a recent development, we’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect. Developed at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in Abu Dhabi, it also supports English, French, Spanish and Portuguese.

In our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used. On our internal Emirati evaluation, it recorded the lowest word and character error rates among the systems we compared.

We also support word-level timestamps for transcriptions, linking each transcribed word to its position in the audio.

Industry observers note that arabic speech varies by region, speaker and setting. A model that handles a formal news broadcast may still struggle with a conversation in Emirati or with speech recorded over a phone line. Dialectal Arabic also has fewer transcribed resources than Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), which makes training and evaluation harder.

According to recent reports, we trained Falcon-ASR on Emirati, MSA, other Gulf and Arabic dialects, and English. Our aim is to transcribe the words people use in everyday speech, including dialectal forms and changes between languages.

The Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard, maintained by the ELM Research Center, ranks systems by the equal-weight average WER across six test sets. It also reports character error rate (CER). Lower values are better for both metrics. Our Falcon-ASR evaluation follows this protocol.

WER = Word Error Rate; CER = Character Error Rate. A lower value indicates better performance.

We evaluated Falcon-ASR on the same six benchmarks using the leaderboard’s pinned manifests. Competitor figures are the published leaderboard averages checked on 30 September 2026. Falcon-ASR’s average WER is 2.25 percentage points better than the best published result in that snapshot.

According to recent reports, public evaluation data already includes Emirati: Casablanca has a UAE subset. We complement that coverage with an internal evaluation of additional Emirati and Gulf speech, using held-out recordings and human-validated transcripts to assess transcription accuracy beyond the public UAE subset.

In our internal Emirati evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved 22.73% WER and 10.19% CER:.

Falcon-ASR has the lowest WER and CER among the systems compared here. Its WER is 4.07 percentage points below Qwen3-Omni, the next best result. The results show improved transcription accuracy at both the word and character level on this evaluation.

We included background noise, overlapping speech, music, room reverberation and telephony effects, as well as variations in speed and pitch. We applied the same treatment to Emirati recordings, exposing the model to a range of conditions it may encounter in meetings, calls and other everyday recordings.

Recent findings suggest that falcon-ASR also transcribes English with the same model weights. In our evaluation on the seven public English test sets used by the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard, it achieved a mean WER of 5.74%.

The model also supports French, Spanish and Portuguese. All five languages use the same weights, without requiring a language flag. The output is a transcript in the language spoken.

Sources indicate that falcon-ASR builds on our Falcon3-Audio work. The architecture and training approach for Falcon3-Audio are described in Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data.

Our Hugging Face Demo Space lets you try Falcon-ASR and explore its transcription capabilities. API access and native applications are planned. We invite you to try the Demo with your own recordings.

We thank the team behind the Falcon-Emirati model for their support with Arabic foundation models. Read about their latest work in the Falcon-Emirati blog post.

We also extend our sincere thanks to Mikhail Lubinets for continued support with the compute infrastructure.

نقدّم Falcon-ASR، نموذجنا للتعرف على الكلام العربي بحجم 1.6 مليار معلمة، مع اهتمام خاص باللهجة الإماراتية. طوّرنا النموذج في معهد الابتكار التكنولوجي (TII) في أبوظبي، وهو يدعم أيضًا اللغات الإنجليزية والفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية.

في تقييمنا، حقق Falcon-ASR متوسط معدل خطأ في الكلمات بلغ 20.92% عبر ست مجموعات اختبار باللغة العربية، مقارنةً بأفضل نتيجة منشورة بلغت 23.17% في نسخة لوحة المتصدرين التي استخدمناها. وفي تقييمنا الداخلي للهجة الإماراتية، سجّل النموذج أدنى معدلات خطأ في الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة التي قارناها.

ندعم أيضاً الطوابع الزمنية على مستوى الكلمات في عمليات التفريغ النصي، بحيث ترتبط كل كلمة بموضعها في التسجيل الصوتي.

يختلف الكلام العربي باختلاف المنطقة والمتحدث وظروف التسجيل. فقد ينجح نموذج في تفريغ نشرة إخبارية رسمية، ثم يجد صعوبة في تفريغ محادثة باللهجة الإماراتية أو تسجيل عبر الهاتف. كما أن الموارد الصوتية المفرّغة نصيًا للهجات العربية أقل من تلك المتاحة للعربية الفصحى، مما يزيد صعوبة التدريب والتقييم.

درّبنا Falcon-ASR على اللهجة الإماراتية والعربية الفصحى ولهجات خليجية وعربية أخرى، إلى جانب الإنجليزية. وهدفنا هو تفريغ الكلمات التي يستخدمها الناس في حديثهم اليومي، بما في ذلك الصيغ اللهجية والانتقال بين اللغات.

ترتّب لوحة المتصدرين المفتوحة الشاملة للتعرف على الكلام العربي، التي يديرها مركز ELM للأبحاث، الأنظمة وفق متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات عبر ست مجموعات اختبار، بوزن متساوٍ لكل مجموعة. وتعرض أيضًا معدل خطأ الأحرف (CER). وكلما انخفضت قيمة أي من المقياسين، كان الأداء أفضل. ويتبع تقييمنا للنموذج هذا البروتوكول.

WER هو معدل خطأ الكلمات؛ وCER هو معدل خطأ الأحرف. تشير القيمة الأقل إلى أداء أفضل.

قيّمنا Falcon-ASR على مجموعات الاختبار الست نفسها، باستخدام قوائم العينات المثبّتة في لوحة المتصدرين. وأرقام النماذج المنافسة هي المتوسطات المنشورة في اللوحة، والتي جرى التحقق منها في 30 سبتمبر 2026. وكان متوسط خطأ الكلمات للنموذج أفضل بمقدار 2.25 نقطة مئوية من أفضل نتيجة منشورة في تلك النسخة.

It has been revealed that تتوافر بالفعل بيانات عامة لتقييم اللهجة الإماراتية، إذ تضم مجموعة Casablanca قسمًا خاصًا بالإمارات. ونكمّل هذه التغطية بتقييم داخلي لتسجيلات إضافية من الكلام الإماراتي والخليجي، باستخدام تسجيلات مخصّصة للاختبار ونصوص مرجعية خضعت لمراجعة بشرية، لتقييم دقة التفريغ على مواد إضافية إلى جانب البيانات الإماراتية العامة.

حقق Falcon-ASR في تقييمنا الإماراتي الداخلي معدل خطأ كلمات قدره 22.73٪ ومعدل خطأ أحرف قدره 10.19٪:.

سجّل Falcon-ASR أقل معدل لخطأ الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة المقارَنة هنا. وكان معدل خطأ الكلمات أقل بمقدار 4.07 نقطة مئوية من Qwen3-Omni، صاحب النتيجة التالية. وتُظهر النتائج تحسنًا في دقة التفريغ على مستوى الكلمات والأحرف في هذا التقييم.

In a recent development, ضمّنا بيانات التدريب ضوضاء خلفية وكلامًا متداخلًا وموسيقى وصدى الصوت وتأثيرات الاتصالات الهاتفية، إلى جانب تغيّرات في سرعة الكلام وحدّة الصوت. وطبّقنا المعالجة نفسها على التسجيلات الإماراتية، لتهيئة النموذج للتعامل مع ظروف مختلفة قد يواجهها في الاجتماعات والمكالمات والتسجيلات اليومية الأخرى.

يفرّغ Falcon-ASR الكلام الإنجليزي باستخدام أوزان النموذج نفسها. وفي تقييمنا على مجموعات الاختبار الإنجليزية العامة السبع المستخدمة في لوحة Hugging Face المفتوحة للتعرف على الكلام، بلغ متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات 5.74٪.

In a recent development, يدعم النموذج أيضًا الفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية. وتستخدم اللغات الخمس أوزانًا واحدة، دون الحاجة إلى تحديد اللغة مسبقًا. ويكون الناتج تفريغًا نصيًا باللغة المنطوقة.

According to recent reports, يستند Falcon-ASR إلى أعمالنا في Falcon3-Audio. وتعرض ورقة Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data بنية Falcon3-Audio ونهج تدريبه.

يتيح عرضنا التجريبي على Hugging Face تجربة Falcon-ASR واستكشاف قدراته في تفريغ الكلام. أما الوصول عبر واجهة API والتطبيقات الأصلية فهو مخطّط له. ندعوكم إلى تجربة النموذج باستخدام تسجيلاتكم.

نتوجّه بجزيل الشكر إلى الفريق القائم على تطوير نموذج Falcon-Emirati على دعمهم في مجال النماذج التأسيسية للغة العربية. ويمكن الاطّلاع على أحدث أعمال الفريق من خلال المقال المنشور حول Falcon-Emirati.

كما نتقدّم بخالص الشكر والتقدير إلى Mikhail Lubinets على دعمه المستمر للبنية التحتية الحاسوبية.

Industry observers note that يعكيكم العافية علي المجهود الطيب... بس بغينا نشوف موديلات صوتية STSو TTS بالللهجة الإماراتية لو أمكن.

#116091. The Next Insider Threat Will Be an Employee’s Personal AI Agent

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1559 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Unite ↗ Open Full Page

The Next Insider Threat Will Be an Employee’s Personal AI Agent

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1559 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, employees are connecting personal agents to work email and Slack faster than security can keep track.
  • Within the next year, employees’ personal AI agents will be working inside most large companies, and most security teams will not know which ones.
  • Sources indicate that the signal arrived in September.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, employees are connecting personal agents to work email and Slack faster than security can keep track. Four questions to help executives get ahead of it.

Within the next year, employees’ personal AI agents will be working inside most large companies, and most security teams will not know which ones.

Sources indicate that the signal arrived in September. Security researcher Patrick Wardle indicated that malware on a Mac could take over a session of Meta’s upcoming Muse assistant and steer it across the victim’s devices. Muse works across files, email, messages and calendar, so whoever controls the session inherits all of it. Meta shipped a fix within a day.

Sources indicate that the flaw matters less than what it exposes. Most conversations about personal agents ask whether the agent is safe for the person using it. At work, the question changes. When an employee connects a personal agent to organization email or Slack, it becomes an autonomous actor inside company systems that security never approved. It has an insider’s access and an insider’s credentials, and none of the controls companies apply to insiders: no background check, no security training, no offboarding. Companies built employee security around people, and the agent acting for each person gets no attention. I expect incidents like this to become routine in 2027.

Four questions separate the security teams in control from the ones guessing.

Which personal agents are already connected to work accounts?

Start here, because everything else depends on the answer. Shadow AI can account for more than 60% of an enterprise’s AI assets, and personal agents add to that share.

Industry observers note that in one deployment, a single employee machine had about 400 agent skills installed, and roughly half of them were malicious. The employee had not chosen them. They came bundled with an AI app installed for work. Public marketplaces show the same pattern: roughly 12% of the skills in one audit were malicious.

It has been revealed that many of these agents run on the desktop, where browser-based monitoring cannot see them. I see the same pattern in customer environments. A tech giant blocks ChatGPT in the browser, so employees download the desktop app or use a personal account. I consider this the most underhyped blind spot in enterprise AI.

Recent findings suggest that blocking has also stopped being the default answer. A year ago, roughly nine out of ten of my customer conversations began with “we do not approve AI in our organization.” Today the question is how to enable employees safely, and that starts with an inventory. The cost of skipping it is documented: 92% of organizations with an AI-related breach lacked proper AI access controls.

Industry observers note that if I had 90 days and one project, I would spend them here. Complete visibility across employee machines, desktops included, is a significant win on its own. In 2027, I expect personal agents to become as ordinary as the browser, so security has to follow the agent down to the individual employee: which agents each person runs, what those agents connect to and what they did.

Are approval and spending limits enforced outside the model?

“Ask me before you spend” is a request typed into the agent. It holds for as long as the agent honors it, and instructions can be forgotten, argued around or overwritten by an attacker.

The stronger design puts the limit outside the model. Even Meta designed Muse so that a separate component, outside the sandbox where the model runs, approves each request, and executives should expect the same arrangement for employee agents.

According to recent reports, tier the limits by risk. Low-risk, reversible actions such as reading a calendar can run automatically. Drafting a reply can run inside defined limits. Moving money, deleting data, sharing files externally and anything irreversible should wait for a person.

According to recent reports, requiring approval for everything creates fatigue and removes the value of the agent. A policy written into the task prompt also falls short. Runtime controls, enforced where the agent cannot edit them, have moved from nice to have to must-have. The industry calls the underlying risk excessive agency: more functionality, permission and autonomy than the task requires. As agents start booking, buying and paying in 2027, I expect transaction authorization to become a major concern. Approval will need to be tied to the specific payee and amount, not to a broad permission to spend granted months earlier.

There is a catch, and Muse demonstrates it too. Meta had this design in place, and the hijack still worked, because the attacker did not need to argue with the agent. It held the agent’s session. Limits outside the model govern what the agent may do. They cannot tell the agent apart from someone holding its keys. That is the job of identity.

Does every agent have its own identity?

Sources indicate that if an agent signs in as the employee, every action looks like the employee took it. Investigators cannot tell whether the person or the agent sent a message, and the company cannot switch off the agent without switching off the person. Shared credentials are one of the biggest violations I see.

Recent findings suggest that personal agents complicate this, because a firm cannot issue an identity to an agent an employee bought on a personal account. It does control the connection point. Access to company email and Slack runs through grants the company can see and govern, so it can require agents to connect through approved apps with their own scoped tokens, refuse connections that reuse the employee’s login and revoke any single grant without touching the employee’s account.

According to recent reports, A separate identity also answers the departure question. Companies have become reasonably good at cutting off access when an employee leaves, but only the access they know exists. An agent with its own identity can be revoked that day.

It has been revealed that scope matters as much, and the Muse flaw demonstrates why: one captured token carried everything the assistant was allowed to do. Read access to one Slack channel limits what a stolen token can do. Access to the whole workspace “just in case” sets the limit at everything.

Moving a credential into a secrets manager improves how it is stored and leaves its scope unchanged. Few teams revisit scope after the pilot, when a token minted for a two-week test quietly becomes the permission the agent runs on indefinitely.

Do you know what normal looks like?

In a recent development, visibility, limits and identity reduce exposure, and they will not catch everything. Teams also need a baseline of how each agent normally behaves: which tools it uses, what data it touches and the order in which it acts. The baseline has to come from the organization’s own traffic, because normal for one organization’s agents looks nothing like normal for another’s.

In a recent development, agent activity differs from human activity in ways a baseline can capture. A person pauses, second-guesses and goes deep on a few leads. An agent moves from reconnaissance to action almost immediately, keeps the same pace at step three and step three hundred, and probes many systems at once.

Sources indicate that defenders hold an advantage here, because context is the one thing an attacking agent cannot shortcut. An attacker’s agent does not know which systems normally talk to each other or which data a given team touches, so it has to probe, and probing looks different from work. You do not need to catch the attack that works. You need to notice the looking.

Respond in steps. Watch the agent, flag it, slow it down, and block only when confident, with unclear cases going to a person. Trust in automated response also depends on explainability. If an analyst cannot see in plain language why an agent was flagged, they will never let automation act alone.

Personal agents will keep arriving, and employees will keep connecting them to the tools they use all day. The leaders who stay in control will find the agents first, enforce limits outside the model, give each agent an identity and learn what normal looks like.

Visibility comes first, and everything else follows from it.

Industry observers note that how many personal agents are connected to your manufacturer’s email and Slack today? If the honest answer is a guess, that is where the first 90 days belong.

In a recent development, ankita Gupta is the Co-founder and CEO of Akto, an enterprise Agentic AI Security and Governance platform helping organizations discover, monitor, and secure AI agents across their environments. She brings 15+ years of experience across cybersecurity, engineering, and enterprise technology, having held roles at JPMorgan, LinkedIn, and VMware. She works with Fortune 1000 enterprises to address emerging security challenges associated with AI adoption, autonomous agents, and the evolving AI threat landscape.

#116089. The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

📅 08 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1559 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

📅 08 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1559 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1.
  • Recent findings suggest that over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way.
  • The first message is where I spend my effort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern, and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16.

Recent findings suggest that over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern plans the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware.

The first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts, exactly as I wrote them.

Industry observers note that A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally claims "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub concerns made the fallback trainer risky.

Industry observers note that two lines in the prompt are critical. The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt claims: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run.

In a recent development, at the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer.

You don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days.

Industry observers note that A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand.

Industry observers note that on the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App.

Recent findings suggest that image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B, trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset.

Sources indicate that the agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model. From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App.

Sources indicate that ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions.

Training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App.

No dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely.

According to recent reports, before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500.

Paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App.

According to recent reports, training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena.

It took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22.

In a recent development, I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37.

Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE.

These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session.

ML-intern is in HuggingChat. Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap.

According to recent reports, if you make something with it, share it on X and tag @Gradio and @HuggingFace. We would love to see the models you make that nobody else would think to build for you.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Nov 23, 2026 3 min read.
  • According to recent reports, securing AI agents is a variation of the insider-risk problem, requiring distinct identities, narrowly scoped credentials and fine-grained policy controls, according to Amanda Walker, senior director of engineering for privacy, safety and security at Google.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: Securing AI Agents in Production.

Nov 23, 2026 3 min read.

According to recent reports, securing AI agents is a variation of the insider-risk problem, requiring distinct identities, narrowly scoped credentials and fine-grained policy controls, according to Amanda Walker, senior director of engineering for privacy, safety and security at Google. In a QCon San Francisco session, she outlined patterns for teams whose agents have been adopted organically and are running ahead of their security and observability frameworks.

With agents now executing multi-step prepares in live production environments, Walker argued that "a rogue AI agent is the same problem as a rogue human insider," one that acts with superhuman speed and persistence. Controls therefore need to work at machine speed, rather than relying on someone reviewing logs the next morning. She covered identity and credentials, boundary defence, subagent orchestration and policy-based containment.

It has been revealed that walker described giving an agent raw human credentials as the fastest path to production failure. The agent inherits the user's authority, so a prompt injection in a document can turn that access to an attacker's purposes. She recommended explicit principals for agents, the AI equivalent of service accounts, so each agent can be provisioned and logged separately without impersonating anyone.

Scoped OAuth tokens limit an agent's access in time and scope, but are immutable once issued. With credential attenuation, an orchestrator instead mints narrower tokens for its subagents, such as read-only access to logs, or read-only access to a repository between two commits when bisecting a broken build.

She pointed to Eclipse Biscuit, a token format whose holders can append restrictions, but cannot remove existing ones without invalidating its signature. It takes more work than reusing human authentication infrastructure, but suits services where teams control both ends.

For API keys, a proxy can give the agent a short-lived synthetic key and substitute the real one as traffic leaves, protecting it from prompt injection and exfiltration.

Walker cautioned that a virtual machine protects the host, not the resources an agent can reach: an agent with network access can still delete a database. Container sandboxes, ephemeral runtimes and sidecar proxies such as Envoy give finer control over file system and network access. But "a perfectly isolated compute sandbox is not useful," she said, so teams need policies that constrain what agents do with the services they call.

She also highlighted poisoned skills on public marketplaces that steal API keys and cryptocurrency wallets, citing Snyk research that found more than a third of publicly available skills had at least one security flaw.

Agents also cause harm by being wrong rather than malicious. Walker described an agent that read internal SRE documentation and invoked a break-glass process intended for emergencies, having decided it was the most expedient route. Monitoring caught it, but the lesson was that organisations must distinguish agents from the people they work for, because some processes depend on a human accepting risk. For the same reason, she described computer-use agents, which drive a mouse and keyboard, as in essence impersonation, while acknowledging they solve problems that machine protocols such as MCP cannot.

Asked in the question-and-answer session about tagging identities as agents, Walker remarked: "The biggest thing it gave us was auditability about some of these risk decisions." The distinction supports human-only rules, such as emergency access, and can help with agent-only rules, such as signed releases in regulated environments, although she noted that an agent flag alone is not enough for those.

In the Q&A, she also advised security teams not to simply say no, which pushes colleagues to work around controls, but to allow experimentation where mistakes are reversible and keep human review for irreversible actions such as wire transfers.

It has been revealed that december 15–16, 2026. Examine how senior practitioners run agents, evals, model serving, and AI-assisted engineering in production, including what failed and what changed. Register Now.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Peptone revealed on November 24, 2026 that its AI- and biophysics-developed prostate cancer candidate, PEP-5089, had entered Investigational New Drug (IND)-enabling development, the preclinical stage supporting an application to begin human trials. The manufacturer also appointed Deepak Sampath as chief scientific officer.

Founder and chief executive Kamil Tamiola remarked PEP-5089 moved from concept to candidate nomination in 18 months, including key in vivo experiments, and that the priority under Sampath’s scientific leadership is to advance the program toward Phase I.

PEP-5089 is an orally bioavailable small molecule that selectively targets the androgen receptor’s intrinsically disordered N-terminal domain, rather than the ligand-binding domain targeted by conventional anti-androgens. That distinction matters for AR-V7, a splice variant that lacks the ligand-binding domain but retains the region PEP-5089 is designed to inhibit.

Peptone reports that the candidate inhibited signaling from both full-length androgen receptor and AR-V7 in preclinical studies, retained activity against all six clinically relevant resistance variants in its ligand-binding-domain test panel, and inhibited tumor growth while substantially reducing prostate-specific antigen levels in prostate cancer xenograft models.

Recent findings suggest that peptone’s program page reports an unbound IC50 of 200 nM for PEP-5089 on its AR-V7 reporter assay, while approved comparators enzalutamide, apalutamide and darolutamide were inactive above 50,000 nM. These findings are preclinical and in vitro, and do not establish clinical benefit.

Sources indicate that sampath previously served as senior vice president and head of research at Ultragenyx after leadership roles at Genentech and Wyeth. His Peptone biography describes more than 25 years of experience across drug discovery, translational science, early development and regulatory submissions, including contributions to the discovery and development of the marketed oncology medicines venetoclax and inavolisib.

Across Ultragenyx, Genentech and Wyeth, he served as project or pharmacology leader for 16 programs that entered IND-enabling studies. Fourteen advanced into Phase I/II trials and six into Phase III, a record directly relevant to the development work Peptone is beginning for PEP-5089.

Recent findings suggest that the company’s pipeline lists PEP-5089 as its only disclosed program in IND-enabling development. PEP-4212, a c-Myc antagonist for MYC-driven solid and liquid tumors, and PEP-3671, a TDP-43 aggregation modulator for ALS and frontotemporal dementia, remain in lead optimization.

Peptone pairs its AI models with experimental measurements of proteins in motion. The company’s technology page describes ultra-fast hydrogen–deuterium exchange mass spectrometry, or HDX-MS: protein and heavy water are mixed in under 10 milliseconds, and the exchange reaction is quenched less than 50 milliseconds later, capturing hydrogen-exchange behavior associated with transient protein structure.

The instrument then fragments the protein and measures the small mass shifts caused by deuterium uptake. Software assembles the fragments into a map of structured and disordered regions over time and encodes that information for Peptone’s AI cluster. Conformational-sampling algorithms propose ensembles consistent with the measurements, exposing potential druggable sites in disordered proteins.

Tamiola stated Peptone built its own hardware and developed proton–deuterium experiments specifically for disordered proteins: “These experiments generate unique data for our AI models, rather than leaving us dependent on existing datasets.”.

Together, the appointment and candidate nomination mark Peptone’s transition from platform-led discovery toward regulated drug development. The next substantive test is the IND-enabling work and, if PEP-5089 proceeds into patients, whether its reported preclinical activity translates into clinical benefit.

Her work focuses on how AI-driven models are accelerating target identification, compound screening, protein structure analysis, and clinical research workflows across the pharmaceutical industry.

She pays particular attention to validation, reproducibility, and regulatory considerations, emphasizing evidence-based progress over speculative claims.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, rahul Pangam is Co-Founder and CEO of RapidCanvas, where he focuses on helping enterprises move AI applications from concept into production.
  • In a recent development, rapidCanvas is a managed AI execution manufacturer that combines an agentic AI platform with field AI engineers to develop and maintain enterprise applications.
  • According to recent reports, before co-founding RapidCanvas, you and Uttam Phalnikar built Simility, which was acquired by PayPal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, rahul Pangam is Co-Founder and CEO of RapidCanvas, where he focuses on helping enterprises move AI applications from concept into production. Before RapidCanvas, he co-founded Simility, which was acquired by PayPal. His work centers on building AI systems that fit real business workflows and remain useful as data, requirements, and operating conditions change.

In a recent development, rapidCanvas is a managed AI execution manufacturer that combines an agentic AI platform with field AI engineers to develop and maintain enterprise applications. Its approach brings together business context, reusable production infrastructure, and ongoing evaluation, with customers retaining ownership of their context, solution IP, and readable code.

According to recent reports, before co-founding RapidCanvas, you and Uttam Phalnikar built Simility, which was acquired by PayPal. What did that experience reveal about the challenges of deploying enterprise AI, and how did it shape your decision to start RapidCanvas?

Fraudsters change tactics the moment you catch them, so a model that was right last quarter can be wrong today. That’s the lesson Simility taught us about enterprise AI. Every customer had different data, risk tolerances and processes, and a wrong call cost real money. Most of our effort went into fitting the system to each customer’s workflow, capturing how their best analysts decided and giving the business enough visibility and control to trust it.

Industry observers note that A platform alone doesn’t make a market. You pick an urgent problem, prove value in production and expand from there. PayPal indicated how much more valuable the technology became once it plugged into existing distribution and infrastructure.

Sources indicate that generative AI made prototypes cheap. Dependable business systems are still hard to build. RapidCanvas covers the full path from business problem to governed production application, so companies don’t have to choose between a tool they staff themselves and a consulting project that never repeats.

Recent findings suggest that gartner predicts that 70% of enterprises will abandon agentic AI built by vendors’ forward-deployed engineers by 2028 because of rising costs and difficulty evolving those systems independently. RapidCanvas also pairs a platform with field AI engineers. What makes your approach different, and where do you agree with Gartner’s concerns?

In a recent development, gartner has the failure mode right. When the field engineer becomes the product, the customer has bought dependency. The context and code sit with a few people outside the tech giant, and every change turns into a upcoming engagement.

In a recent development, our engineers have two jobs: capture the business context a generic platform can’t see, and turn repeated work into product. Each deployment should make the next one less custom. They start from reusable production infrastructure and domain patterns, and the customer’s definitions, rules, workflows and decision history live in an Enterprise Context Engine the customer owns.

In a recent development, customers also own their solution IP and get readable code. They can run in their own cloud, a managed environment or SaaS, and nothing ties them to one model provider. We stay accountable after go-live without making the customer dependent on us. The test is whether the customer can see what the system knows, how it’s evaluated, what it’s allowed to do and how to change it. If the answer is no, Gartner’s concern is justified.

You emphasize that your engineers remain accountable after applications go live. What does that accountability mean in practice when an application’s accuracy declines, business requirements change, or the expected financial return fails to materialize?

In a recent development, too many vendors declare victory at go-live. That’s when our job really starts, because running software and valuable software are two different things.

It has been revealed that before launch, we agree with the customer on the business outcome and the technical bar. We test on their own data, set benchmarks with known answers and turn those criteria into a regression suite. After launch, we track accuracy, groundedness, human acceptance, errors, latency, cost and adoption. When performance slips, we diagnose the whole system before blaming the model. The cause could be data drift, a schema change, a upcoming business rule, a prompt, a model upgrade or a workflow we never captured correctly. Every fix has to clear the same bar before people see it.

Industry observers note that when the financial return doesn’t show up, the model, the workflow or the business hypothesis is wrong, and each calls for a different response. We might recalibrate, narrow the application’s authority, redesign the process, swap in conventional automation or stop the use case. Keeping a project alive because everyone is invested in it is the worst outcome. AI has to earn its place in the operation.

RapidCanvas offers custom AI applications through subscription pricing. How do you keep costs predictable as customers add integrations, increase usage and request changes, and what are the limits of what the subscription covers?

Predictable pricing comes from productizing the repeatable work and being upfront about what varies.

Industry observers note that customers pay a flat monthly subscription based on their exact needs. It covers customized solutions built with our experts, full platform access, user licenses, integrations, monitoring, maintenance, support and training. They can add or drop solutions and build new ones on the platform without opening a services project every time the business changes. That works because we reuse tested infrastructure and domain patterns, use deterministic software where it’s the better tool and route each task to the model with the right balance of accuracy, latency and cost.

Recent findings suggest that the price does assume a defined user population, deployment model, infrastructure footprint and support level. If a customer materially expands any of those, or moves into a upcoming data environment, we agree on the change before the economics shift. Normal evolution of an agreed solution stays in the subscription, while a materially new footprint is a commercial conversation. Customers should never see a change order for the routine work of keeping production AI useful.

In a recent development, your Enterprise Context Engine captures business processes, rules and decision history. How do you turn undocumented employee knowledge into context an AI system can reliably use, particularly when people disagree about how a process should work?

Tribal knowledge only becomes usable context once it has a source, an owner and a decision rule. Dumping transcripts and documents into a large context window just creates a bigger pile of unstructured data.

According to recent reports, we start with what the company already has: documents, system records, schemas, procedures and decision history. Then our engineers sit down with process owners and frontline employees to capture what those systems miss, including definitions, exceptions, approval paths and the reasons behind judgment calls. The Enterprise Context Engine turns all of it into structured, versioned context. Every fact traces back to a source, and every rule carries an owner and a change history.

Industry observers note that when people disagree, that tells you the process was never standardized. The system surfaces the conflict, and we work out whether it reflects a legitimate variation by region, product or business unit or whether the manufacturer needs one approved rule. A named process owner decides, and we record the decision, exceptions, effective date and approval. Until the business resolves it, the AI shouldn’t pretend it has. That call stays with a person.

Sources indicate that how do you decide whether a customer’s problem needs an autonomous agent, a predictive model or conventional automation? Can you share an example where a simpler approach proved more effective than an agentic system?

The most mature AI architecture usually has less AI than people expect. Each approach should do the job it’s best at.

Recent findings suggest that conventional software or rules should carry most of the load when the logic is stable, repeatable and explainable. A predictive model may be enough when the business needs a forecast, score or probability. Agents make sense for workflows that involve multiple steps, changing information, tool use and judgment within clear limits. Most serious applications combine all three, with people keeping authority over the highest-stakes decisions.

Invoice reconciliation shows why. One customer had to reconcile invoices across 15 entities and eight currencies. Most of that work called for normalization, matching logic and consistent rules. AI added value on the ambiguous cases, and people reviewed the exceptions. The application went live in three months and now matches more than 90% of invoices automatically. A fully autonomous agent would have added variance to a process that depends on exactness. The goal is the best business outcome with the least unnecessary complexity.

According to recent reports, reusing components across deployments can improve economics, but each business has different requirements. Which parts of an AI solution can you safely standardize, and how do you validate that a component proven for one customer will work for another?

Sources indicate that standardize the scaffolding and leave the judgment to the customer. Every enterprise application needs production engineering, and very little of it is unique to any one tech giant.

In a recent development, we standardize authentication, role-based access control, data connectors, deployment, audit logging, security scanning, monitoring, testing, error handling and the evaluation harness. We also reuse domain patterns for recurring problems like invoice reconciliation, document extraction and forecasting. That gives every engineer a real head start.

In a recent development, what stays customer-specific is the business context: terminology, data shape, thresholds, approval hierarchy, exceptions, risk tolerance and outcome measures. We treat reuse as a hypothesis. A component that worked for one customer gets us to validation faster but never lets us skip it. Every deployment is tested on the customer’s own data against acceptance criteria for that workflow, including edge cases, access controls, security, load and end-to-end behavior. Reuse shortens the time it takes to produce evidence, and the evidence bar stays where it was.

What testing and monitoring should an enterprise require before allowing an AI application to take consequential actions? How do you handle model updates, unexpected behavior and decisions that need human approval?

Sources indicate that autonomy is a delegation decision before it’s a model decision. Companies already have rules for delegating authority to people, and AI needs the same discipline.

Before an application takes a consequential action, the manufacturer should define what the system can see, what it can recommend, what it can do on its own and what needs approval. Each task type needs an acceptance threshold, examples from the customer’s own data and a trace from every output back to its source, rules and model. The application also needs access controls, end-to-end and load testing, a named owner, an audit trail and a rollback path.

In high-stakes workflows, recommending and acting should be separate steps. Payments, claims, regulated decisions, material financial commitments and unusual exceptions go to a person until the evidence supports more autonomy. Model updates should be handled like software releases, with any latest model, prompt or schema change clearing the same regression suite first. If behavior turns unexpected, the system should stop or narrow its actions, route the case to review and roll back if needed. Autonomy gets earned one workflow at a time and stays revocable.

RapidCanvas states more than 40% of its customers now run multiple AI use cases in production. Could you walk us through a customer’s progression from its first deployment to broader adoption, including measurable results and anything that did not work as expected?

That 40% is the number I watch most closely. A successful pilot is good evidence, but the real proof is a customer asking for a second and third use case because the first one changed how the business runs. Here’s what that looks like in practice.

Recent findings suggest that one North American channel incentive management platform started with claims processing. We captured the rules behind the workflow and built controlled paths to approve, hold, adjust or reject each claim. The decision engine now applies 499 business rules and has processed more than 11,000 claims. In one recent quarter it adjudicated 494 claims, approving 297, declining 77 invalid ones and holding 84 for review.

Recent findings suggest that once that workflow was stable and the customer could see how decisions were made, the relationship grew to four use cases across claims adjudication, program intake and fraud mitigation. Each new one started with the context, controls and infrastructure the first had already established.

Not everything moved at the same pace. The fraud work stayed in design longer because the outcome definition and telemetry weren’t ready, and we had no results we were comfortable claiming. I’d rather delay a use case than automate something we can’t yet evaluate. A good first deployment doesn’t make every neighboring process ready for AI.

As AI automates more application development, how will the role of field AI engineers change? What expertise should enterprises retain internally so they can understand, govern and eventually modify their systems without becoming dependent on a vendor?

It has been revealed that code is getting cheaper, which makes judgment worth more. Field AI engineers will write less of the undifferentiated foundation and spend more time understanding the business, choosing the architecture, defining evaluations, designing exception paths and setting controls.

The role moves toward architect, adviser and validator, and the technical work becomes more consequential. The key skill is knowing where AI belongs, where deterministic software does better, what evidence to require and how the system should behave when it’s uncertain. The strongest engineers will translate between domain experts, data, software and governance, with no single model at the center.

Recent findings suggest that enterprises don’t need to build an AI lab, but they should keep the expertise a model can’t replace. That means a business or product owner accountable for the outcome, domain owners who know the exceptions, data and architecture leadership, security, risk and compliance expertise and enough engineering skill to inspect the code, integrations, configuration, evaluations and change history. The customer should own the durable assets: its context, solution IP, readable code, evaluation suite and change-control record. A good partner leaves the enterprise more capable after every deployment and never becomes indispensable.

Thank you for the great interview, readers who wish to explore an enterprise AI platform and implementation expertise for automating business workflows should visit RapidCanvas.

Latest Update: Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that firefox on iPhone is growing fast across the world.
  • But there remains an vital limitation to what is available on iPhones: Apple forces all browsers on iOS to be built on Apple’s own browser engine.
  • According to recent reports, this has meant that companies like Mozilla cannot easily bring the full range of Firefox features and functionality to iPhone owners because many of these are built within our browser engine, Gecko.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that firefox on iPhone is growing fast across the world. This is especially true in the EU since 2024, when the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) started requiring Apple to let people choose their default browser; millions have picked Firefox, and daily use on iOS has doubled. People want to choose the browser on their phone.

But there remains an vital limitation to what is available on iPhones: Apple forces all browsers on iOS to be built on Apple’s own browser engine.

According to recent reports, this has meant that companies like Mozilla cannot easily bring the full range of Firefox features and functionality to iPhone owners because many of these are built within our browser engine, Gecko. iPhones and iPads are unique in having this restriction. On all other major operating systems, including Apple’s macOS, people can access the Gecko-powered version of Firefox.

As a result of the DMA, Apple began allowing alternative browser engines on iOS in the EU. It published a set of conditions that companies like Mozilla must comply with to bring their own browser engine. At the time we mentioned Apple’s rules made it “as painful as possible” for alternatives like Gecko. In the meantime, Japan also introduced new rules requiring alternative browser engines on iOS. Apple applied very similar conditions in Japan to those in the EU.

Nearly three years since Apple introduced these conditions in the EU and almost a year since Japan, not one developer has been able to launch a non-WebKit browser on iOS. The reason is simple: Apple’s conditions remain unworkable. The real test of any rule is whether it delivers the change it was meant to achieve in practice. Compliance on paper alone falls short of that test.

According to recent reports, since the DMA came into effect we’ve been working behind the scenes to test and improve Apple’s conditions so that we can bring Gecko to iOS users. Those efforts have so far largely failed.

In a recent development, one of the conditions requires us not to disclose non-public information related to the project, but here’s an example of what we are up against: to use Gecko, we can’t simply patch the Firefox app people already use and love. We’d have to build a whole separate app, a second Firefox. Then we’d have to ask every Firefox user to download it, move their bookmarks, passwords and history across, and manually switch over, step by confusing step.

That’s a lot to ask of people who already made their choice. A significant proportion of people would understandably give up, including many who picked Firefox from the EU’s choice screen.

The conditions Apple imposes, including a level of user friction Apple would never accept for its own apps, mean that the open door feels more like a trap door.

Firefox users on iPhone chose an independent browser. They should get everything that comes with it, including Gecko, the last major browser engine not developed by a big tech company. We’ll keep pushing for a real level playing field, not an opening that drops independent browsers through the floor.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device.
  • LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA.
  • Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:.

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

According to recent reports, for your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0):.

Industry observers note that serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:.

Recent findings suggest that the port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

Both LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meta added its Muse personal AI agent to Instagram direct messages on November 24, 2026, announcing through Muse’s verified Instagram account that users can send it a DM to “turn your saves into real plans,” with a trip they have been meaning to take as the example.

Sources indicate that the addition gives Muse a conversational entry point inside Instagram alongside its other chat surfaces. Meta’s Muse product site describes chatting through the Muse app on mobile or desktop, or directly in WhatsApp, by message or voice. It separately lists Instagram among the apps that can be connected to the agent, with users deciding what Muse can see and do.

In its September 8, 2026 launch post, Meta said Muse could organize Instagram Saves and create artifacts such as travel guides from them, with Instagram connected as one source of context. The initial standalone rollout was in the US on iOS, Android and the Muse website.

Sources indicate that that workflow reflects Muse’s intended difference from a conventional chatbot. Meta describes the agent as remembering conversations, proactively working toward goals and suggesting ideas, rather than only answering isolated questions. The DM entry point connects task initiation with the place where the content was saved. For Meta, the product significance is a shift from Instagram as a source of context to Instagram as both a source and a place to delegate work.

According to recent reports, meta’s account infrastructure already links some of these services. Its connector documentation says Facebook, Instagram and Threads connect automatically when the accounts share an Accounts Center. While connected, Muse exchanges information relevant to the tasks assigned to it. Users can manage those accounts through Accounts Center.

In a recent development, private-message access has a more specific boundary. Meta’s security and privacy page indicates Muse does not read private messages unless the user grants access through private-messaging connectors or Muse on Mac. Permissions are set per connector, and users can read, edit or delete what Muse remembers. The upcoming DM surface lets someone message Muse; it does not, by itself, alter that documented rule for reading private messages.

Actions beyond retrieving information carry another set of controls. Meta’s approval guide distinguishes read actions, such as checking a calendar or reading an email, from write actions, such as sending a message or making a purchase. Users can require approval before every write action and notable read actions, or before any action, and inspect a chronological activity log. Some actions can be stopped or undone in chat, but a sent email cannot be reversed.

Sources indicate that disconnecting a connector stops future data exchanges, but information previously used for tasks may remain in Muse’s memories and conversation history. The data-control guide indicates stored interactions can include text, voice, photos and information obtained through connectors. Deleting material also does not necessarily erase information Muse learned from it.

Users can delete individual messages and side chats, ask Muse to forget a topic or set of interactions, or reset the agent to permanently delete its chat history, files and active tasks. The setting allowing interactions to help train Meta’s AI models is on initially, and turning it off also applies to previous interactions. The result is a more direct route from saved Instagram content to delegated work, with permissions and retention settings determining how far that delegation extends.

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

Recent findings suggest that pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

With several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:.

According to recent reports, add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

Sources indicate that boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

Sources indicate that for edits, each region states where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:.

According to recent reports, everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

It has been revealed that black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:.

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

In a recent development, A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call.

According to recent reports, let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:.

It has been revealed that FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

Recent findings suggest that so one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

It has been revealed that this gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:.

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

Industry observers note that in stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Industry observers note that every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Recent findings suggest that each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

According to recent reports, the noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

The distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Sources indicate that attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:.

Text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

Recent findings suggest that at every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps highlights how the image takes shape:.

Industry observers note that the fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are new to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[ demo | about | screenshots | design | docs | code | warning! | contact | credits | links ].

9/UX brings the classic Mac and A/UX desktop (a spatial desktop, a global menu bar, consistent controls and dialogs, icons, and resource-driven presentation) to 9front, built the Proposal 9 way: rio and libdraw draw the screen, 9P exposes every application's UI state and commands as files, namespaces define the working environment, the plumber opens documents, and ndb holds human-editable metadata.

It is not an emulator, a Macintosh ABI, or an A/UX reimplementation. Native 9front programs stay first-class, and existing rio programs (acme, sam, rc windows, nested rio) keep working unchanged beside 9/UX apps.

According to recent reports, these are real frames, not mockups. The GUI tests embed h9 with a headless screen, inject mouse and keyboard input, and drive the 9P files at the same time.

Industry observers note that macintosh structure, Proposal 9 colour: butter title bars from rio's selection yellow, acme's cream and olive, and rio's greygreen for the desktop, so 9/UX windows and legacy rio windows sit together on one screen. Everything reads in one bit, uses a sixteen-colour palette, and is drawn in whole pixels. Every graphic is original to 9/UX; it ships no Apple resources. The mockups below are generated from the same palette and metrics files as the code.

Sources indicate that the design document describes 9/UX and its v0.1 acceptance criteria; release.md has where each one stands, the end-to-end demo, and the open issues. Every interface between components is a file protocol in docs/protocols, and the visual design covers the palette, fonts, metrics, chrome, icons and cursors.

Sources indicate that the source is on GitHub, under the MIT license. Development runs on h9, which runs 9front's own compilers, mk and rio directly from the host shell, without booting a VM. scripts/h9.sh clones and builds the pinned h9 on its first run:.

Use rio/6.out on amd64. development.md and testing.md have the details.

Sources indicate that 9/UX is at v0.1 and under active development. Interfaces and behaviour change without notice.

Please report bugs and send questions through GitHub issues.

In a recent development, the 9/UX mark in the menu bar is a pixel-art Glenda by Dan Fessler. Glenda, the Initiative 9 bunny, was created by Renée French.
